context.text: Boccioni was a central painter, sculptor and writer within Italian Futurism. His work explored how art might convey movement and the passage of time. Early paintings engaged with urban life, while encounters with Cubism encouraged increasingly fragmented forms. His manifestos and objects were connected attempts to give a changing modern world a new visual language.

Bonheur made animals the sustained focus of her painting. Trained by her father, she drew at horse markets and built an international reputation through works such as The Horse Fair. Direct study was an important part of that practice. Her success also challenged the restrictions placed on women's professional lives in nineteenth-century art.

Bonnard began within the Nabi circle, alongside his lifelong friend Vuillard, and went on to make domestic life a sustained field of experiment. Interiors, gardens, flowers and figures offered familiar subjects through which to explore colour. His wife appears repeatedly, including in bathing scenes, as the people and places around him became material for a deeply personal art.

Bosch worked in 's-Hertogenbosch, where he belonged to an established family of painters and a religious brotherhood. His fantastic creatures have often encouraged speculative accounts of his beliefs. The paintings are more securely approached through the devotional literature, proverbs and imagery of his time. Conventional Christian subjects form a substantial part of his work alongside the crowded visions for which he is best known.

Botticelli worked chiefly in Florence, drawing on the example of his teacher Filippo Lippi. Flowing contours and finely controlled gestures became central to his art. He painted for churches, civic patrons and members of the Medici circle, and contributed to the Sistine Chapel decoration in Rome. His religious and mythological subjects share an interest in the expressive possibilities of line.

Bronzino trained with Pontormo in Florence and retained a close relationship with him. Their early work can be difficult to distinguish. From 1539, service to Cosimo I de' Medici made court portraiture central to Bronzino's career. His polished surfaces and controlled poses give visible form to the splendour and ceremony of that world; his friendships with writers also informed his portrait practice.

Ford Madox Brown combined brilliant colour and painstaking detail with a strong sense of painting's moral purpose. His subjects included contemporary work and emigration as well as historical narratives. He shared the Pre-Raphaelite circle's commitment to nature without becoming a formal member of the Brotherhood. His independent career also embraced decorative design and large murals on Manchester's history.

Caravaggio gave religious and secular subjects an arresting physical presence. His figures often occupy a shallow space close to the viewer, with strong light making bodies and gestures stand out against darkness. The directness of his religious imagery sometimes troubled its commissioners, even as collectors sought his work. His paintings helped establish a new naturalistic approach that artists across Europe adapted in different ways.

Carpaccio developed religious stories through elaborate settings and a strong interest in everyday incident. His cycles devoted to Saint Ursula and to Saints George and Jerome gave those qualities room to unfold across many canvases. Venetian life enters the narratives through architecture, costume and crowded activity. The individual paintings reward attention both as episodes and as parts of a larger sequence.

Petrus Christus developed a particular interest in placing figures within clearly defined interiors. His portraits and religious paintings draw on Jan van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden, while simplifying some of their forms. He became a leading painter in Bruges in the generation after van Eyck. The often-repeated account of a formal apprenticeship with him remains unproved.

Church studied with Thomas Cole and expanded the Hudson River School's ambitions through extensive travel. South American mountains, tropical vegetation and northern ice became subjects for large paintings that attracted substantial public attention. His work combines the appeal of spectacular scenery with an interest in distant environments. The scale of a finished canvas could turn a view into an event for its audience.

Constable found his strongest subjects in places he knew well, especially Suffolk and Hampstead. He studied earlier landscape painters closely while seeking a more immediate account of changing light and weather. Outdoor oil sketches fed paintings developed in the studio; for his largest canvases he also made full-size painted studies. Rough touches of paint could suggest sunlight, wind or rain with a freshness that unsettled some early viewers.

Correggio worked mainly in northern Italian centres away from Rome and Venice. His early paintings suggest close study of Mantegna; later, Leonardo's softly modelled forms helped shape his fluid handling of figures. Altarpieces and smaller devotional pictures form an important part of his work. Their tenderness and intimacy accompany an increasingly sophisticated sense of movement and light.

Sánchez Cotán painted still lifes in Toledo before entering the Carthusian order in 1603. His arrangements of fruit and vegetables use precise spacing and strong contrasts with darkness. Ordinary objects acquire a concentrated presence through this careful organisation. Religious painting also formed part of his career, though it is the still lifes that most clearly distinguish his work.

Courbet gave ordinary people and familiar landscapes the scale and weight usually reserved for elevated subjects. Study of earlier painters helped shape his strong modelling, but his relish for paint's physical substance was distinctly his own, often expressed with a palette knife. His Realism challenged accepted hierarchies of art. Political involvement later brought imprisonment and exile, yet landscape and portraiture continued to sustain his painting.

Working alongside Pissarro in the early 1870s encouraged Cézanne to study nature closely and brighten his palette. He exhibited with the Impressionists while pursuing his own concern with pictorial structure. In landscapes, portraits and still lifes, subtle changes of colour help build weight and space. Repeated visits to a subject allowed him to develop a painting through sustained observation rather than a single impression.

David's study in Rome helped him develop the clear forms and moral gravity associated with Neoclassical painting. Back in Paris, ancient history became a way of addressing duty and public virtue. His involvement in the French Revolution extended to politics and the design of public festivals. The paintings therefore belong both to a classical artistic tradition and to urgent arguments about contemporary power.

Degas brought a rigorous training in drawing to subjects such as dancers, laundresses, racecourses and the theatre. He exhibited with the Impressionists but had little interest in their emphasis on outdoor landscape. Cropped figures and unexpected viewpoints can make his pictures feel momentary, yet they were carefully composed. Painting, pastel and drawing offered him different ways to revise and develop a subject.

Literature, history and music were lasting interests for Delacroix, and his subjects ranged from ancient myth to Shakespeare and contemporary events. A major figure of Romanticism, he also devoted substantial energy to large decorative commissions. His work links the ambitions of public mural painting with a highly personal engagement with stories, colour and dramatic feeling.

Van Dyck learned much from Rubens in Antwerp, then developed a distinctive approach to portraiture during six years in Italy. Titian's example helped him give aristocratic sitters an elegant, commanding presence. That approach served him again at the court of Charles I in London. His portraits shaped how later generations pictured the English court and influenced British portrait painting well beyond his lifetime.

Dürer's early training connected the goldsmith's workshop with painting and book illustration. Prints helped carry his work to a wide audience, while travel brought him into contact with other artistic traditions. His repeated self-portraits also assert an ambitious view of the artist's profession. Their carefully constructed public identities are part of a career in which practical craft and intellectual inquiry developed together.

Jan Brueghel specialised in richly coloured landscapes and still lifes, particularly flowers. His finely differentiated textures earned him the nickname Velvet Brueghel. After working in Italy he settled in Antwerp, where collaboration became an important part of his practice: he contributed landscapes, animals or flowers to paintings made with Rubens and other artists.

Cranach's early paintings combine figures with richly observed landscape. His long service at the Saxon court brought portraits, religious commissions and mythological nudes into a busy workshop that repeated popular designs. In Wittenberg he supported Martin Luther and produced portraits and illustrations for the Reformation, while also accepting Catholic patrons. His output reflects the overlapping demands of faith, courtly display and a market for elegant figures.

Bruegel's village scenes belong to a much wider body of work that includes religious subjects, landscapes and designs for prints. He lived in major cities and worked for cultivated patrons; the nickname 'Peasant Bruegel' describes some of his subjects, not his social position. His Alpine travels left a lasting mark on his landscapes, while humour in his art often coexists with suffering and indifference.

Ensor turned masks, skeletons and grotesque figures into a language of social and religious satire. These subjects emerged from an earlier practice of vigorously painted domestic interiors. Based almost entirely in Ostend, he developed an art that crossed the concerns of Symbolism and Expressionism and later interested the Surrealists. His strange crowds make familiar public life seem at once theatrical and threatening.

Jan van Eyck served Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, as a painter and in diplomatic roles. His closely observed portraits and devotional paintings established an influential model for later Netherlandish artists. Oil painting existed before him; his achievement lay in what he could make the medium do. Precise surfaces and convincing figures helped bring painted spaces into an unusually immediate relation with the viewer.

Fragonard trained with Boucher and then spent several years in Rome. There he was drawn to freer, more colourful painting, including Tiepolo's example. Scenes of courtship and pleasure became an important part of his work. Their lightness depends on lively handling and inventive arrangement, as much as on the subjects that link him with Rococo art.

Piero della Francesca brought a remarkable clarity to relationships between figures, architecture and space. Monumental forms and lucid perspective coexist with subtle colour and light. He worked for religious and courtly patrons while keeping close ties to his native Sansepolcro. His surviving writings on mathematics and perspective show that the construction of pictorial space was a sustained intellectual concern as well as a practical one.

context.text: Friedrich made landscape a setting for contemplation, often giving sea, mountains or winter fields an unusual stillness. His paintings could carry religious feeling without telling a biblical story. Figures seen from behind invite the viewer to share their act of looking, while also remaining inaccessible as individuals. Observation and inward reflection both mattered to the images he constructed.

Gainsborough earned his living chiefly through portraiture, while continuing to paint landscapes for his own pleasure. Moving from Ipswich to Bath brought grander commissions and encouraged a freer, more elegant portrait manner. Even after leaving the countryside, he developed landscapes in the studio, sometimes using arrangements of twigs and stones. Observation and invention both shaped those settings.

Gauguin left stockbroking to paint full time in 1883. At Pont-Aven he developed emphatic outlines and areas of colour that served expressive and symbolic purposes rather than simply matching appearances. His later career took him to Tahiti and the Marquesas. The paintings belong to his search for an alternative to European artistic conventions, and should not be treated as straightforward records of island life.

Gauguin, Paul.places: Paris, Brittany, Tahiti and the Marquesas

context.text: Artemisia Gentileschi trained in her father Orazio's workshop but developed a more forceful, dramatic style. Biblical narratives became a particular strength, with the story of Judith among her recurring subjects. She built a reputation across Europe and, in 1616, became the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia del Disegno. Her career took her from Rome and Florence to Naples and, for a period, England.

Giorgione gave colour, landscape and atmosphere a new importance in Venetian painting. His intimate pictures for private collectors can make mood more immediately compelling than a clearly identifiable story. Only a small group of works can be confidently attributed to him, yet his influence was profound. That combination of artistic impact and fragmentary evidence helps explain the continuing debate around paintings associated with his name.

Giotto made bodies feel weighty and gestures carry the force of a story. His religious scenes use a convincing sense of space to bring figures into direct, emotionally charged relationships. The frescoes in Padua's Arena Chapel are central to understanding this achievement. His approach influenced generations of Italian painters, who found in his work a model for joining physical presence to narrative clarity.

Hugo van der Goes combined meticulous surface detail with a commanding organisation of figures and space. His religious paintings can convey intense feeling through individual faces and gestures. The Portinari Altarpiece carried that approach to Florence, where its handling of oil and its vividly characterised shepherds influenced local painters. His career spanned civic work in Ghent and continued painting after he entered a monastery near Brussels.

Van Gogh committed himself to art in 1880, after working in the art trade, teaching and religious ministry. His career lasted only a decade, sustained by extraordinary effort and his brother Theo's practical and emotional support. The apparent immediacy of his work should not obscure its thoughtfulness: he read widely, planned his paintings carefully and discussed his decisions at length in letters.

Goya's career ranged from lively tapestry designs and court portraits to disturbing images of violence and superstition. His portraits combine social distinction with an unusually direct sense of individual presence. Work made outside official commissions gave his imagination greater freedom: the prints and the late Black Paintings explore subjects far removed from courtly display. The variety matters as much as the darkness for which he is now famous.

Baldung's work combines brilliant colour with expressive changes to the human figure. His varied output includes religious painting, portraits, allegory and designs for prints and stained glass. Dürer was an important early connection, but Baldung developed a distinct interest in unsettling subjects, including witchcraft. Those themes form part of a broader practice rather than defining all of it.

Guercino's early paintings use forceful brushwork, rich colour and dramatic light to give figures an energetic presence. His stay in Rome from 1621 to 1623 encouraged a more classical direction, which became stronger after his move to Bologna in 1642. The calm, lighter manner of his later paintings differs markedly from his youthful work. His lively drawings reveal another side of his invention, extending beyond studies for finished compositions.

Hals spent most of his life in Haarlem and worked chiefly as a portrait painter. He gave both individual sitters and civic groups an unusually lively presence. Gestures and fleeting expressions matter as much as formal pose, while energetic handling contributes to the impression of people caught in conversation or movement. His portraits are carefully made images, even when their animation suggests spontaneity.

Hopper found subjects in the rooms, streets and roadside buildings of modern America. His spare settings and reserved figures often suggest isolation without supplying a definite story. Light and the arrangement of space remain central to their effect. His distinctive vision developed in etching as well as in oil and watercolour.

Ingres treated drawing as more than a means of describing a body. A contour could have an expressive rhythm of its own, even when it departed from ordinary proportions. His career combined a commitment to the classical tradition with highly personal distortions that sometimes baffled critics. Portraits, drawings and large figure compositions all reveal this tension between disciplined finish and inventive line.

Kandinsky left a career in law and moved to Munich to study art in 1896. He became an important theorist as well as a practitioner of abstraction. Series titled Impressions, Improvisations and Compositions explored increasingly independent roles for colour and line. The musical language reflects a sustained interest in how visual relationships might convey feeling without depending on a recognisable subject.

Klimt moved from successful public decoration to a leading role in the Vienna Secession, founded in 1897. After controversy over his university paintings, private patrons remained important to his career. In many portraits and allegories, recognisable faces and bodies meet densely patterned clothing or backgrounds. That interplay between the figure and the decorated surface is a defining feature of his mature art.

Lucas van Leyden worked in painting and stained-glass design, but his engravings and woodcuts gave his art a particularly wide European audience. Dürer was an important influence, and the artists met in Antwerp in 1521. His later paintings also incorporated ideas from Italian art. Prints were a major means through which those artistic connections developed and circulated.

Filippo Lippi's early paintings draw on Masaccio's substantial figures, but his later work gives greater prominence to flowing line and decorative detail. Delicate light, patterned fabrics and fluttering drapery bring a distinctive intimacy to his religious subjects. A Carmelite friar, he painted both large fresco cycles and smaller devotional panels, especially images of the Virgin and Child. His example was important to Botticelli.

Claude combined close observation of the countryside around Rome with carefully composed, ideal landscapes. Light gives these invented settings their unity: cool mornings and warm evenings establish a mood across water, buildings and trees. Biblical and mythological figures often inhabit the views. His paintings had a lasting influence on landscape art and even on the design of English country estates.

Lotto was born in Venice but worked in several centres, including Bergamo and towns in the Marches. His painting drew on both Italian and northern European examples. Portraits made his acute observation especially visible, while religious commissions formed the larger part of his career. The variety of settings and patrons helps explain why his work sits somewhat apart from a single Venetian model.

Malevich developed Suprematism after exploring the fragmented forms of Cubism and the movement of Futurism. Geometric shapes and colour could, he believed, free painting from the need to depict familiar objects. The apparent simplicity of these works carried an ambitious search for sensation and boundless space. He later returned to figurative painting, bringing some of those experiments into recognisable bodies and rural subjects.

Manet brought his study of the Old Masters into paintings of contemporary Paris. Their modern subjects and abrupt contrasts of light and dark challenged expectations at the Salon. Younger painters admired him, but he continued seeking official recognition and never joined the Impressionists' group exhibitions. His later work nevertheless shared some of their interest in outdoor light and a brighter palette.

Mantegna's work reflects the humanist culture of Padua and a sustained fascination with antiquity. Firm drawing and adventurous foreshortening give his figures a sculptural presence. As court painter to the Gonzaga in Mantua, he also explored how painted architecture could transform a real room. His art brings close study of the ancient world together with an inventive command of pictorial space.

Marc helped develop the Blaue Reiter circle with Kandinsky and other artists. Encounters with French painting encouraged him to move beyond naturalistic colour. Animals became central to his search for a spiritual relation with nature: he saw them as less compromised than human beings. The unusual colours of his animal paintings belong to this expressive ambition, rather than to a wish for literal description.

Memling settled in Bruges and developed a successful workshop serving local and international patrons. His painting is closely related to Rogier van der Weyden's, though a formal apprenticeship is not securely documented. Restrained feeling and balanced arrangements characterise many of his devotional works. Portraiture gave him another field in which to develop an attentive, carefully controlled manner.

Modigliani developed much of his career in France, drawing on Renaissance painting, Cézanne and his own experience of sculpture. Elongated forms and simplified features give his portraits and nudes a distinctive rhythm. His stone heads and paintings share an interest in reducing a figure without losing its presence. Most of the paintings for which he is known belong to the last five years of his life.

Monet's interest in outdoor painting began with encouragement from Eugène Boudin and Johan Barthold Jongkind. Changing light remained a central concern throughout his career, pursued both outdoors and through work in the studio. His series returned to a subject under different conditions. At Giverny, the garden he created became a sustained source of paintings, especially of the water-lily pond.

Morisot made modern figure painting a field of bold experiment. Quick strokes, broken contours and areas of lightly covered canvas give her interiors and outdoor scenes a feeling of immediacy. She often painted women in the settings of everyday life, exploring how a figure relates to the surrounding space. She helped organise the Impressionist exhibitions and participated in seven of the eight.

Murillo worked chiefly in Seville, where religious commissions were central to his career. His early paintings use strong contrasts of light and dark; the mature work often softens figures and atmosphere. Subjects such as the Immaculate Conception gave him ways to express Catholic doctrine through accessible, emotionally appealing images. That devotional purpose helps explain the idealisation of many of his figures.

O'Keeffe developed enlarged flowers and plant forms into paintings that approach abstraction while retaining their natural starting point. Broad shapes and rhythmic contours also appear in her landscapes. Her subjects extended to New York architecture, linking parts of her work with Precisionism. These different settings share an interest in making familiar forms newly conspicuous through scale and selection.

Jacob Cornelisz van Oostsanen helped establish Amsterdam as a centre of painting and print design in the early sixteenth century. His religious paintings combine close observation with inventive decorative detail. Woodcut designs, including a series of Christ's Passion, gave his art another form and audience. He belonged to a family of artists and was also known as Jacob van Amsterdam.

Giovanni di Paolo worked in the Sienese tradition, drawing on artists including Gentile da Fabriano and Sassetta while developing a highly personal manner. Small religious panels form much of his surviving work. Figures inhabit landscapes that can feel strange and imaginative rather than simply topographical. That relation between devotional narrative and invented setting is part of his distinctive appeal.

Patinir helped give landscape a new prominence in European painting. Religious figures remain important to his subjects, but extensive settings can command most of the viewer's attention. His rocky terrain has often been connected with the Meuse region, although his early life is poorly documented. The paintings balance recognisable stories with a growing independence for landscape itself.

Sebastiano brought a Venetian feeling for colour to the ambitious figure painting of Renaissance Rome. His early work was close to Giorgione's, but after moving to Rome in 1511 he formed a lasting professional relationship with Michelangelo, who supplied drawings for some commissions. Monumental religious paintings and portraits became important parts of his practice. The portraits often give their sitters an imposing, sombre dignity.

Pontormo developed from Andrea del Sarto's example towards a highly individual approach to figures and space. Restless movement, surprising changes of scale and unstable-looking arrangements helped place him at the forefront of early Mannerism. His compositions can be emotionally charged even when their subjects are familiar. The tension arises from the way bodies, colour and space interact.

Potter specialised in animals within landscapes, making cattle and other rural subjects the focus of sustained attention. His paintings range from small scenes to the life-size scale of The Young Bull. Close description of the animals and their surroundings helped give these subjects an importance usually reserved for other kinds of painting.

Poussin treated painting as a carefully ordered language of action and feeling. Working mainly in Rome for private collectors, he drew on ancient literature, biblical stories and the example of earlier masters. Preparatory drawings and small staged models helped him study composition and light. His search for clarity gave figures and gestures a deliberate weight, shaping the classical tradition in French painting long after his death.

Raphael's early work absorbed Perugino's graceful drawing and gentle expressions. In Florence, encounters with Leonardo and Michelangelo helped him develop more complex, unified groups; in Rome, those skills served ambitious papal commissions. The clarity of his compositions can make elaborate arrangements look effortless. His expanding workshop also became essential to the large volume of work produced during his short career.

Rembrandt trained in Leiden and with Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam, whose example encouraged his interest in biblical and mythological narrative. After settling in Amsterdam in the early 1630s, he quickly established himself as a portrait painter. Across these subjects, light and gesture could give figures both dramatic purpose and individual presence, bringing narrative energy even to a formally commissioned group portrait.

Renoir began by decorating porcelain before training in Paris alongside Monet, Sisley and Bazille. Scenes of contemporary leisure and outdoor light helped him develop Impressionism. In the 1880s, studying Italian art encouraged a search for firmer outlines and more solid figures. He later returned to softer handling and warmer colour, often painting nudes and figures removed from a specific moment of modern life.

context.text: Repin made Russian history and contemporary social life major subjects for ambitious painting. Portraits, scenes of labour and criticism of political abuses all belong to his range. A period in Paris brought him into contact with new approaches to colour and light, but he remained committed to art's moral and social purpose. That commitment helps explain the seriousness he gave to ordinary people's experience.

Rigaud's portraits helped define the public image of the French court under Louis XIV. Pose, gesture and dress present the sitter's rank with carefully organised grandeur. Alongside these formal commissions, he made more intimate portraits, including studies of his mother. The contrast shows how deliberately his manner could change with the purpose of a picture.

Rubens developed his art during eight years in Italy, studying antique sculpture and painters from the Renaissance to his own day. Back in Antwerp, he organised a large studio to meet international demand. Assistants and specialist collaborators contributed to many commissions, with his own involvement varying from design to extensive painting. He also worked as a diplomat, connecting artistic patronage with European court politics.

Ruisdael gave Dutch landscape an unusual range and emotional force. Woodland, dunes, grain fields, mills and waterfalls all appear in his work, often built from dense colour and strongly modelled forms. Observation and invention work together: he painted Scandinavian torrents through other artists' example and could transform a modest hill into a commanding height. His landscapes shape our experience of a place as much as they record its features.

Sargent's training and career were international, with important roots in Paris and a lasting admiration for Velázquez and Frans Hals. He became widely sought as a portraitist, using fluent brushwork to describe both a sitter and the display of clothing and setting. Later he reduced his portrait commitments, devoting more time to watercolours and large decorative projects.

Andrea del Sarto combined balanced figure groups with a particularly sensitive handling of colour and atmosphere. Based in Florence, he worked on fresco cycles, altarpieces and portraits. His drawings reveal the preparation behind that apparently fluent manner. Artists including Pontormo trained in his workshop, where the poise of the High Renaissance helped provide a starting point for later Mannerist experiments.

Schinkel is best known as an architect, but painting and stage design were central to his early career. His Romantic landscapes belong to an imagination concerned with the relationship between buildings, scenery and the viewer's experience of a place. These connected practices developed before his major appointment in the Prussian building administration in 1815.

Serov's portraits range from informal likenesses to grand society commissions, painted with freedom and assurance. He studied with Repin and at the St Petersburg Academy before becoming a leading Russian portraitist. His work also includes landscape, scenes of everyday life, historical painting and illustration. That range helps explain the flexibility he brought to a sitter's pose, setting and public presence.

Seurat developed his painting through sustained study of drawing, colour theory and earlier artists, including Delacroix. He explored the idea that separate touches of colour could produce a different luminosity from pigments mixed together. His carefully organised compositions belong to that investigation. The drawings, with their broad areas of dark and light, reveal another side of the same concern with visual relationships.

Titian worked across portraiture, religious painting and mythology, bringing rich colour and a strong sense of movement to very different commissions. His early work developed close to Giovanni Bellini and Giorgione; his mature career connected Venice with courts across Europe. Oil paint gave him a flexible means of describing flesh, fabric and light, and his increasingly broad brushwork sometimes challenged his patrons' expectations.

Toulouse-Lautrec made the cafés, music halls and nightclubs of Montmartre central to his work. His scenes can feel like sudden glimpses, but their apparent spontaneity rests on sustained drawing. Degas and Japanese prints helped shape his use of oblique viewpoints and unexpected compositions. Thin oil paint, sometimes applied to cardboard, let him give figures a striking presence with economical means.

Turner's career began in drawing and topographical watercolour, before he expanded into oil painting. He established himself early at the Royal Academy and remained deeply conscious of the landscape tradition. Works made in homage to earlier painters could also challenge them. This relationship with the past is part of his inventiveness, alongside his experiments with the expressive possibilities of light and atmosphere.

Vasnetsov's early paintings dealt chiefly with contemporary life, including the urban poor. From about 1880 he turned increasingly to Russian history and legend. In these subjects, researched details of dress and setting support an imaginative reconstruction of the past, giving myth the presence of a fully inhabited world.

Velázquez began in Seville with closely observed figures and objects, then entered Philip IV's service in Madrid in 1623. Portraiture became central to his court career. Studying paintings in the royal collection, especially Titian's, helped him develop a lighter palette and freer brushwork. The contrast between a convincing presence at a distance and economical touches of paint is one of his work's enduring attractions.

Vermeer worked in Delft, producing a small surviving body of paintings. His domestic interiors often use a few figures, carefully organised spaces and light entering from one side. Their quiet appearance is built through varied handling of paint, including broad touches that can disappear in reproduction. His household also depended on the art trade, and financial pressures became severe during the Dutch economic crisis of the 1670s.

Leonardo sought unity between figures and their surroundings through subtle transitions of light and colour. His use of sfumato softens boundaries so that forms seem to emerge from atmosphere. Experiment was central to his practice, sometimes at a material cost: the technique he tried for The Last Supper proved unstable. His surviving paintings make up a small part of a much broader activity in drawing and investigation.

Waterhouse began with subjects from the ancient world and increasingly turned to literature in the 1880s. His romantic narratives share interests with the Pre-Raphaelites, while his handling of paint is generally broader and richer than their early method. Stories gave him settings for absorbed or emotionally charged figures. He belongs to a later reworking of that tradition.

Watteau brought the worlds of theatre and elegant leisure into a new kind of painting. His scenes of fashionable figures in parkland became known as fêtes galantes. Drawing from life supplied a repertory of poses that he could reuse in different compositions, while small touches of colour animate the surface. A feeling of passing pleasure gives these carefully invented gatherings a distinctive, sometimes melancholy atmosphere.

Rogier van der Weyden gave religious scenes an emotional intensity sustained by tightly organised compositions. Grief and tenderness register through faces, hands and the arrangement of bodies. Working in Brussels, he maintained a busy workshop, and his paintings and designs circulated widely across Europe. His influence outlasted knowledge of his life: many details of his career and the attribution of individual works still depend on careful comparison.

Grant Wood gave scenes of Midwestern life a distinctive pattern of sharply defined forms and meticulous detail. His study of early Netherlandish paintings during a visit to Munich in 1928 helped move him away from an earlier Impressionist manner. Working chiefly in Iowa, he became a leading Regionalist. His paintings range from portraits and stylised landscapes to imaginative or satirical treatments of American history.

Zurbarán worked chiefly on religious commissions, especially for churches and monastic communities. His saints and monks often have a strong physical presence, established through simple arrangements and concentrated light. This directness could serve both devotional intimacy and the public expression of Catholic belief. Still lifes and a smaller number of secular subjects show the range of the same attentive naturalism.

This panel was never meant to hang on its own. It was the central cult image, the focus of devotion, of an altarpiece to Saint George. Four smaller scenes of the saint's gruesome martyrdom once flanked it, two stacked on each side, and those are now in the Louvre in Paris. As was usual in Catalonia, a Crucifixion would have crowned the whole, and a base painted with smaller stories would have carried it. Martorell, the leading Catalan painter of the early 1400s, set the graceful, ornate manner called International Gothic beside a few sharply realistic touches.

No document records who ordered it. The museum's 2004 catalogue names the Catalan government, the Diputació, as almost certainly the patron, with the government's own chapel of Saint George, put up in the 1430s, as the intended home. The museum's object page is more careful: Martorell probably painted it for that chapel, in the Barcelona palace of Catalonia's government, and George is the region's patron saint. Surviving pieces of the chapel's decoration, including an embroidered altar frontal, share related imagery, and the government had documented dealings with Martorell. The museum dates the panel 1434–35.

As late as 1867 the centre and its four side scenes were still lent out together in Barcelona. In 1917 the panel was sold to Charles Deering, of Sitges near Barcelona and of Chicago, and his daughters gave it to the Art Institute in 1933. The altarpiece had even lent its painter a name: he was once known only as the Master of St George. A group of paintings, this one among them, is now given to Bernat Martorell on grounds of style. Just one surviving work of his, an altarpiece of Saint Peter dated 1437–42, is securely documented.

details.text: Look up at the castle. Under a red canopy, on a balcony draped with a patterned red cloth, a crowned king and queen watch, while townspeople in pointed and rolled hats pack the battlements and windows. Lower down at right the princess, crowned and in a pink, fur-lined mantle, raises her hands, and a sheep grazes beside her. In the legend the town kept the dragon quiet with two sheep a day, then a person with each sheep when the flocks ran short, until the lot fell on the king's own daughter.

Now find the dragon's cave, the dark opening in the rocks at right. Small grey creatures cling to the stone around its mouth: lizards, or perhaps baby dragons. The sandy ground below is littered with what is left of earlier victims, the bones of animals and people, a horned skull at lower left and a human skull at the bottom edge.

The gold is not flat. Martorell built up gesso and carved it in relief before gilding the saint's halo, his weapons and the horse's harness, so they are raised from the surface and give the panel a sculptural quality. The dragon's scaly hide is raised the same way, though painted rather than gilded, and the sand of the foreground has its own gritty texture.

context.text: This man is praying to a picture that is no longer there. His panel was once one half of a small folding diptych, made to be carried about. His eyes and joined hands were aimed at the other half, which shows Mary with the infant Jesus and is now in Tournai's Musée des Beaux-Arts in Belgium. Such paired panels probably began around 1400 as pictures for royalty. They stood for prayer that never stopped, and they kept a record of the donor's face. Rogier van der Weyden gave the type fresh life in the mid-1400s, painting diptychs for people at the very top of the Burgundian court.

His name comes from the back of the panel. It carries his coat of arms, his initials JG on either side of the shield, and his motto on a ribbon: 'GRACES . A DIEV.' He is Jean Gros, who served the future Duke of Burgundy as an administrator. The portrait, from around 1460–64, shows him near the start of a career that brought him great wealth and a life of privilege. Ordering such a diptych advertised his ambition and his close ties to the duke's circle. From 1469 he was secretary to Charles the Bold. He has been called greedy, in office and in business alike.

The two halves went separate ways. The portrait passed through collections in Bruges and Paris. In 1912 the New York collector Benjamin Altman paid $47,000 for it, then handed it back to the dealer that November. Martin Ryerson of Chicago bought it in 1913 for $33,785 and left it to the Art Institute in 1933. The Virgin had a rougher time. In the 1920s the restorer Jef Van der Veken worked it over so hard that it is now called a 'hyper-restoration'; he even painted in fake cracks of age. In 1941 it was sold to Hermann Goering. Allied troops found it at Berchtesgaden, Belgium got it back in 1946, and Tournai has held it since 1951. Gros's arms on its back still match the ones on his.

details.text: Look at the hands. They rise into the picture from below, palms pressed flat, fingers pointing up, and his gaze slides off to the left of the frame. On their own they pray to no one. Beside the Virgin panel they became a prayer addressed to her.

Now look at the face with its owner in mind. The panel is the work of Rogier together with his workshop. One reading holds that Rogier left more of it than usual to his assistants, perhaps because he disliked the sitter, and did the same with the Virgin panel. The same reading finds that showing Gros at prayer only makes his face look more worldly.

context.text: This panel was with a family in Jaén, in Spain, by 1956 at the latest, and probably earlier. In May 2015 the family sold it at auction in Madrid. A Dublin company, Goldengate Arts, bought it; that October it passed to Colnaghi and Coll y Cortés in London and Madrid. In 2016 it went to the Art Institute of Chicago.

Devotional images of Jesus carrying the cross were much in demand in the sixteenth century, and Sebastiano del Piombo painted the subject many times. In Rome in the 1510s he was pulled into the rivalry between Michelangelo and Raphael. Michelangelo took him up, taught him his monumental manner and gave him drawings for his commissions. Sebastiano was Pope Clement VII's favourite painter.

details.text: Look at the two men pressing in behind Christ. One is Simon of Cyrene, who tries to help him lift the heavy cross. The other is a Roman soldier who only looks on with menace. The soldier is the man in the steel helmet; the young man gazing upward is the helper.
The cross cuts across the panel in strong diagonals. Past its arms, at upper right, a dim landscape opens under a reddish sky, and far off on a hill a small cross already stands.

context.text: Is he getting up to speak to someone, or pointing at a thing we cannot see? Lotto caught this man in mid-gesture, arm flung out and head turned, and what the gesture means has never been settled. Freezing an interrupted moment like this is typical of Lotto. It sets the picture apart from the stiffer Italian Renaissance portraits elsewhere in Cleveland's collection.

Who he is depends on which clue you follow. The plants on the table suggest a wedding: clover meant plenty, luck and a happy marriage, and jasmine meant purity and love, a message the roses on the trellis repeat. On that reading there may once have been a companion portrait of his bride, the woman he is declaring his devotion to. Another reading names him as Girolamo Rosati, who held high office in Fermo, on the east coast of Italy. If so, the paper might be a plan for one of his major building projects, and the hand might be pointing to it far off.

It once belonged to the imperial collection in Vienna and came to Cleveland in 1950. Lotto signed the canvas at lower right, but the date breaks off after '15'. Cleveland places it in 1533–34; it has also been dated around 1525 and called simply a portrait of a nobleman.

details.text: Look at what he wears. The heavy gold chain, the sword at his waist and the rich, fashionable clothes all broadcast money and rank at a glance.

Now look at the table and the lattice behind the balustrade. Loose sprigs with small white flowers lie by the paper, and pale blooms hang among the trellis slats. These small plants carry the marriage reading.
The raised hand is set against open sky. That particular blue became one Lotto treated as his own.

context.text: This scroll was probably painted for a man about to retire, a fellow official of Guo Xi's, and probably late in the painter's own life. It dates from about 1080, or perhaps a few years earlier, in the late 1070s. One later reader was still tied to his desk. Zhao Mengfu (1254–1322) left a short poem on it, about mountains and rivers too hard to catch in ink and the life among woods and streams he had always wanted. Then: "Constrained by petty official duties, I have been unable to achieve it."

Guo Xi's own name is missing: there is no signature or seal of his anywhere on the scroll. Later writers added their own lines. Yu Ji (1272–1348) ended his verse with a question: "So I ask on this painting by master Guo, How is Mr. Shi Donggao?" A further inscription also names a Shi Donggao, calling him a route commander, and says the scroll's materials come from between the Baoyuan and Yuanyou eras (1038–1093). After three hundred years, it says, they have returned to Shi Donggao's writing table. With its mounting the scroll is over eight and a half metres long. The painting takes up just over one.

details.text: Look at the left end, where the scroll finishes. Two elderly figures cross a little plank bridge towards a pavilion on the rise, each with a smaller attendant at his side. They may be going to say goodbye to a friend, along with colleagues; another account has them simply off on an outing. Higher up the slope, two more small figures carry things up to the pavilion.

Now look at the trees. Their trunks twist, their twig ends hook, and almost no leaves are left, with mist gathering behind. It reads as late autumn. Bare trees, two elderly walkers, perhaps a farewell: and the scroll itself was probably made for a man leaving office.

context.text: Nobody can be sure who painted Summer Mountains. It used to be given to Yan Wengui (active about 970–1030). But no painting by Yan is recorded in the collection of Emperor Huizong (r. 1101–25). The emperor's painting catalogue does list three works called Summer Scenery by Qu Ding, a follower of Yan's in the eleventh century. The scroll is now attributed, tentatively, to Qu Ding. Beyond those titles he is otherwise unknown, though one account makes him a court painter under Emperor Renzong (r. 1022–63).
Texture strokes and ink washes this advanced suggest a master of about 1050. Seals of Emperor Huizong, who owned the scroll, fit that date.

details.text: Read it from right to left, the way a handscroll is meant to be viewed. It opens on a fishing village by the river. Look at lower right for the tall masts of large boats moored along the shore, while small skiffs come home from the day's outing. Mist fills the woods, perhaps after a summer shower, perhaps on a midsummer evening.

Travellers head towards a temple retreat. The tiered roofs among the trees below and to the left of the tallest peak may be that retreat, though another reading places it at the far left end. The peak rules the scene the way an emperor rules his subjects: it is the top of nature's order. Two tiny figures cross a little bridge just right of centre, near the bottom. Viewers are meant to put themselves in their place, walking towards the mountain.

context.text: These two small birds are credited to an emperor whose love of art, in one historian's view, blinded him to the danger his country was in. Huizong (1082–1135), eighth emperor of the Song dynasty, ruled from 1100 to 1125 and was the most gifted artist of his imperial line.

Academy painters copied his pictures, and the lucky ones got his cipher written on their copies; his work and theirs can now hardly be told apart. This scroll carries his cipher and two of his seals, Yushu and Xuanhe. It is catalogued as his own, in the new academy manner of the Xuanhe years, 1119–25.

The picture is about 55 centimetres wide; mounted, the scroll runs to 8.39 metres, carrying inscriptions by later owners and viewers. Zhao Mengfu (1254–1322) wrote: "What good fortune for these insignificant birds to have been painted by this sage." The Ming collector Xiang Yuanbian (1525–1590), who paid heavily for it, was harder on the emperor. He had only played at a minor skill, Xiang wrote, and ended up a captive in the north.

details.text: Look at the lower bird. Sleek, wings and tail drawn back, it tips its head up towards the bird on the higher spray. One reading takes them as a male singing to a female who looks coyly away, though here the upper bird turns its head right, towards him.

Now look at the eyes. Each is a tiny drop of lacquer, a last touch to make the birds seem alive. Xiang Yuanbian wrote that the emperor dotted eyes in raised black lacquer, so the birds looked ready to take off.

The bamboo is read as a bright spring morning: leaves green again after a hard winter, pink tendrils sprouting from each branch, though here they look tan. One reading sees in this neat, ordered growth the dream of a ruler shut away from a troubled world.

context.text: Banished by the emperor Domitian to Patmos, a Greek island, the young John is writing the Book of Revelation in the volume on his knees. Above him the Virgin appears in a vision, as the woman of that book, "clothed with the sun, and with the moon under her feet."

Baldung had trained in Dürer's workshop in Nuremberg and opened his own in Strasbourg in 1509. This panel was once one of three that made up an altarpiece ordered by a religious order there. It has been proposed that the patrons were the Order of Saint John, then based at Grünen Wörth just outside the city. Records of payments to Baldung in the order's accounts for 1510–11 fit that idea. If so, the patrons moved in 1687 into Saint Marx, a cloister inside Strasbourg. By the time of an inventory there in 1741, the three panels were listed separately, probably taken apart earlier during troubled years at Grünen Wörth.

For the composition, Baldung turned to an engraving by Martin Schongauer of 1469–74, which also puts the saint in the lower right corner gazing up at an apocalyptic vision of mother and child in the sky.

details.text: Look at the eagle at lower left. It is John's emblem, and it stands on a precious book, a sign of the inspiration from above that drives him to set down what the vision shows him.
On the rock to the right of John's robe, low down, is a tiny monogram. Baldung began signing his works this way only after 1510.

Now look at the crescent under the Virgin's feet. It was laid in white metal leaf, now strengthened with restoration paint. Elsewhere, the mottled brown in places across the landscape and foliage is a common discolouring of paint made with copper greens.

context.text: Cranach dresses an ancient beauty contest in the armour of his own day. He was a celebrated court painter to the electors of Saxony at Wittenberg. Pictures of Venus, especially the Judgment of Paris, were among the most popular myths that he and his workshop turned out for courtly patrons. In this version of about 1528, Paris sits in a full suit of plate as he decides which goddess is the most beautiful: Juno, Minerva or Venus.
By 1922 the panel belonged to the Munich collector Marczell von Nemes, who lent it to the Germanisches Nationalmuseum in Nuremberg for two years. The Met bought it at his sale in Amsterdam in 1928.

details.text: Look at what the bearded man is holding. He is Mercury, and in the story the prize is a golden apple. Cranach has turned it into a clear glass ball.
Look up at the cloud at top left. Cupid is drawing his bow on Venus, a sign that Paris will choose the goddess of love. The picture does not show which of the three women she is.

context.text: Three half-length figures and a bare green ground: Dürer kept this picture plain. His stay in Italy in 1505–7, chiefly in Venice, had fed his taste for deep colour, careful detail and simple forms. From about 1518 he seems to have pushed further toward simple, solid figures, and this panel is a case in point.

The panel probably stayed in Nuremberg with the Tucher family, its owners from about 1519, into the early 1600s, and by 1630 it belonged to Elector Maximilian I of Bavaria. Its arrival at the Met came with a condition. Benjamin Altman paid Duveen $228,890 for it in 1911 and left it to the Met in 1913, on terms under which it may not be lent.

details.text: Look at the right edge, level with Mary's hair: a small gold 1519 above Dürer's AD monogram. Both were added later. Even so, the year is thought likely to be right.

Look at Anne, the Virgin's mother, a saint especially honoured in Germany. Her wide eyes look straight out of the picture, not at her daughter or grandson. That outward look can be read as a foreboding of Christ's Passion. Read that way, her hand on Mary's shoulder becomes a gesture of comfort.

context.text: The oldest king has set his crown on the ground. Kneeling, he lifts the newborn Christ out of the manger himself. Adorations very rarely, if ever, show this. No written text is known behind it. Still, devotional writing of the thirteenth century encouraged a similarly human way of telling the sacred story, and so did liturgical dramas and mystery plays.

The panel was never meant to hang alone. It was one of seven scenes painted side by side on one horizontal plank, split by thin gold bands; the others are now in Boston, Munich, Florence and London. Saint Francis kneels at the cross in the central Crucifixion, so the set was surely made for a Franciscan church. Which one has never been proven. The date is open too: one proposal is about 1305, but most place it in the 1310s or 1320s.

Its author has shifted as well. It sold in London in 1839 as a Giotto and in 1874 as Early Italian School. The Met once listed it as by Giotto's workshop; today it credits Giotto. The series ranks among the finest that workshop produced, and most scholars think Giotto himself had a large hand in it.

details.text: Look at Mary and Joseph. He holds out the king's gift and stares. She, propped on her mattress under the roof, wears a worried look.

At top left, an angel swoops down to two shepherds with news of the birth, so Luke's shepherds and Matthew's Magi share one panel. It may be the earliest Florentine painting to join different Nativity episodes. The spiky star in front of the hill was added later.

context.text: She has the room; he has only a window. A woman stands inside, her profile filling most of the panel, while a man peers in at her through an opening at the side. No Italian painting older than this one survives that joins two sitters in a single portrait, that sets them at home, or that looks out onto a landscape. Lippi kept the usual profile pose for both of them, but he painted their hands as well. The two are not equals in the picture. She dominates the space; he is pushed outside it, off to the side, a watcher.

Who they were is still an open question. His hands rest on a shield with the arms of the Scolari, a Florentine family. From those arms the pair were tentatively named as Lorenzo di Ranieri Scolari and, as his bride, Angiola di Bernardo Sapiti, a couple whose wedding is usually placed around 1436, though later research found the two still unmarried in 1439. A newer proposal reads the arms as hers rather than his. It names Francesca di Matteo Scolari and Bonaccorso di Luca Pitti, married by 1444, and suggests that Bonaccorso's father, Luca Pitti, may have ordered the picture. Her costly clothes, her many rings and an embroidered motto all suit a bride, although the panel could instead celebrate the birth of a child.

Several of Lippi's altarpieces include portraits of their donors, and comparison with them puts this panel at about 1440–44, the years of his Annunciation now in Rome. Some earlier studies preferred 1435–36. Another moved it to the 1460s because of her headdress; that view has been rejected, partly because the arms do not belong to the man it proposed. For decades the picture carried another painter's name. The Reverend John Sanford bought it in Florence around 1829, and his inventory listed it as a Masaccio. It was lent to the Royal Academy in London in 1877 under that name, and in New York in 1888–89 it was still shown as a Masaccio "Female Head". Henry G. Marquand gave it to the Metropolitan Museum in 1889.

details.text: Look at the man's hand above the shield, its forefinger lifted. Lippi first painted him with a hand raised just under his chin, in mid-gesture, as if speaking to her rather than merely watching. The shield came later, painted over the ledge, and the left edge of the window frame was adjusted. Today only the forefinger is clearly lifted, but the final gesture has been read as the horned hand, with forefinger and little finger raised. It is often taken as the sign of a cuckold, but it could also mean blessing and protection. Infrared examination shows that her hands were rethought too, laid one over the other so that she looks modest and composed.

Now find the band of gold and pearl embroidery on her cuff, beside her folded hands. The embroidery is read as lealtà, loyalty. Her dress follows French fashion: a red overdress edged with pale fur, a dark brocade sleeve flecked with gold, a pearl necklace, a brooch at the shoulder and rings on her fingers. The tall headdress is a type called a sella alla fiamminga, worn from the second quarter of the 1400s into the 1470s. He is dressed just as expensively, and his red hat marks his high standing.

Through the second window, behind her face, a small landscape opens up: a house with a red roof, a path or stream lined with dark trees, buildings and hills beyond. It may show land the family owned. Then look at the wall just behind the man's profile, where a faint darker band follows its outline: the shadow of his face. Pliny told how painting began when a lover traced the outline of a beloved's shadow, and Lippi may well have had that story in mind. On that reading the panel celebrates love and beauty as much as it marks a betrothal, a wedding or a birth.

context.text: Mantegna made the Virgin and Child a kind of doorway between earth and heaven. Her blue and gold robes run on into clouds, where cherubs whirl about the newborn child. The picture may have been made for Borso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara. Its style looks like an answer to the taste for Netherlandish painting in that city. Still, nobody can show for certain that Borso ordered it.

The owner dates it shortly after 1450. That it belongs to the 1450s is broadly agreed, although most scholars place it in the middle or later years of that decade. It may be the picture listed in 1586 with Margherita Gonzaga, Duchess of Ferrara, as a "Prosepio de Andrea Mantegna", a Nativity by Mantegna.

It was painted on wood. In 1927 the paint was moved from the panel onto canvas, a transfer that badly damaged the edges. Even so, the paint surface itself remains in exceptionally good shape, and traces of the original raised border and its red painted outline survive all the way round. It had often been said that the picture was cut down. A microscopic examination in 2009 showed that it was not.

details.text: Look at the two shepherds on the right. Their clothes are ragged and of the painter's own day. One presses his hands together in prayer; the other has pulled off his hat, and both are on the point of kneeling. Joseph, asleep on the left, is dressed instead in classical drapery, which sets him off against the two newcomers.

Now look at the woven fence behind Joseph. A squash hangs over it. It may refer to the paraduro, a heraldic device of the Este family, which is one reason the picture has been linked to Borso. Above, the ox is busy with a mouthful of grass. Mantegna left out the ass.

The child lies on the hem of his mother's robe, boldly foreshortened, and the cherubim around his head have their faces picked out in shell gold. Beyond them a river winds away past a tall grey crag. Giovanni Bellini repeated that river and rock in his own Dead Christ, now in Milan.

context.text: Three separate panels, one world. Joachim Patinir laid a single landscape across all three parts of this triptych, with a horizon that runs unbroken from wing to wing, and gave each part its own sacred story up front. As an altarpiece, the triptych needed those stories. They were also his excuse for the wide panoramas that made him famous.

Follow the land from left to right. Forbidding peaks give way to bright yellow-green rolling hills, then to a broad sheet of water that calls to mind the lush Schelde estuary at Antwerp and carries on into the right wing. As the eye travels back, the colours cool from green to blue, a use of atmospheric perspective typical of him.

On the outside of the wings, not shown here, Saint Sebald appears in grisaille. He was Nuremberg's patron saint, so the triptych was very likely made for patrons in southern Germany. Emperor Leopold I of Austria owned it until 1674. Then the Austrian monastery of Kremsmünster kept it for more than two and a half centuries, until 1935.

details.text: Look at Saint Jerome in the centre. He kneels with his chest bared and a stone raised in his fist, punishing his own body as he pleads with Christ. The crucifix on the ground in front of him is tiny, but in his mind the Christ on it is alive. The monastery he founded near Bethlehem sits further back, up on a high plateau.
In the left wing Christ stands in the river Jordan to be baptized. Further back, under the trees, Saint John preaches in the wilderness to a crowd gathered in front of him.

At the right, Saint Anthony the Hermit holds a book and a rosary in his left hand while monsters in the manner of Bosch push in behind him. Look above them for the owl perched on a bare branch. Owl and monsters alike point to the saint's struggle against Satan's temptations.

context.text: For decades this Annunciation was taken for a masterpiece by Rogier van der Weyden, and it entered the Met as a late Rogier in 1917. An early challenge, since taken up by others, argued instead for the young Hans Memling, who arrived in Bruges on 30 January 1465. In 1998 the museum's catalogue hedged, calling it Rogier's workshop, possibly Memling. Today the Met credits Memling himself. The design is a free adaptation of the left wing of Rogier's Columba Altarpiece in Munich.

The patron left his mark on the picture. A pair of linked keys (clés unis) is shown on the shield in the stained glass and once more on the carpet, and they belong to the Burgundian Clugny family. The patron was most likely Ferry de Clugny, a leading lawyer, a member of the Duke of Burgundy's Grand Council and a notable patron of art. The painting must be earlier than 1477: in that year Louis XI made Ferry a bishop and the family arms were changed. Ferry founded the Chapelle Dorée at Autun in 1465, and one tempting idea is that the panel was made for it. Whether he first asked Rogier, who died before he could take it on, or went straight to Memling, cannot be settled.

At about 186 by 115 centimetres the panel is unusually big for a Netherlandish painting of its time. Tree-ring study shows Baltic oak, with two boards cut from one tree, and suggests a date of 1456 or later. Before it entered the Met's collection, someone shaved the panel down to only 2 millimetres and fixed a supporting cradle at the back. It was once thought to be the left wing of a huge triptych; it now seems more likely that it always stood alone.

details.text: Look up at the top of the window. The blue shield in the glass carries the two joined gold keys of the Clugny family. The same keys are woven into the carpet at the bottom of the panel, under the hem of Mary's mantle.

Mary's left hand holds a lit wax taper wound into a coil, resting on her open prayer book. The underdrawing shows a different first idea: a tall candlestick stood on the prayer desk, and one page of the book was drawn lifted, as if being turned. Both were left out when the panel was painted.

Gabriel comes dressed in the church vestments of a deacon. Around Mary the room is full of signs about her. The lilies in the gold-coloured jug stand for her purity. The walled garden outside stands for her chastity, and so does the greenish glass carafe on the shelf at top left, since light passes through it unbroken.

context.text: Giovanni Borgherini ordered this picture when Florence had thrown off the Medici and made itself a republic, if the date of about 1528 is right. Proposed dates run from about 1526 to about 1530. Its central gesture carries the republic's politics. Saint John the Baptist, the city's patron saint, hands the orb to the Christ Child. The message is that Christ, and no Medici, is the one ruler of Florence. One reading ties this to a teaching of Savonarola: that the city had moved its allegiance from the Baptist to Christ as its king.

Vasari described the Borgherini picture as having a Madonna, "a little S. John offering to Christ a globe that represents the world, and a very beautiful head of S. Joseph." Copies followed, and some were confused with this one. On the strength of Andrea's studies in the Louvre and the Uffizi, the Met's panel is taken to be the primary version, the one painted for Borgherini. Its later story is less clear. Medici papers record Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici buying a picture from a Vincenzo Borgherini in 1579, while the Met's provenance lists this one with Vincenzio Borgherini, perhaps until 1597.

details.text: Look at the hands around the globe. The Baptist holds it from below, the Child reaches in to take it, and the old man's hand rests on top.
Look at the old man behind the globe, gazing straight out. He is Saint Joseph, and one reading takes his head for Andrea's own face.

context.text: Even a plum tree rotten with age flowers at the very start of spring. That made it a sign of endurance and renewal. Here a single old tree fills four gold sliding doors. Together they made up a whole wall at Myōshinji, the great Zen complex in Kyoto, in a room of its subtemple Tenshōin: probably a reception room where the abbot lived. Each of the room's four sides most likely had its own giant tree. On their backs, facing the next room, was a Chinese subject, the Eight Daoist Immortals. That side is now in the Minneapolis Institute of Art.

The doors are thought to be by Kanō Sansetsu, probably from the end of his career. They date from 1646, or perhaps 1647, the year the building they were made for went up; they were likely finished with it. In 1647 the court also gave Sansetsu the title of Hokkyō. His last years were spent under a cloud all the same. He was imprisoned for a crime he believed he had not committed.

Around 1886, so the story goes, the temple let the doors go to pay for repairs after a fire. They then moved between collectors in Kyoto. Even the black lacquer frames are probably later. One of those owners must have added them when he cut the doors down to suit his smaller house.

details.text: Look at the trunk. It climbs out of the right-hand doors, arches up and left over the middle two, and comes down again in the second door, dark and knotted. Thin twigs spray from it, carrying small pale blossoms across the gold: the old tree still flowering in the cold.
The joins hide a loss you cannot see. At least a foot of painting is gone where the first door meets the second, and again where the third meets the fourth. The tops were trimmed as well.

context.text: Kōrin's sea does not sparkle. It grabs. Its crests curl like a dragon's talons, and the whole screen feels faintly threatening. That dark streak is unusual for him. One reading ties it to his unhappiness in Edo (now Tokyo), where he lived in the service of a daimyo, a feudal lord.

The screen is now generally thought to date from between 1704 and 1709, while Kōrin was living in Edo. In Edo he could look closely at old ink paintings by Sesshū and Sesson, monk-painters of Japan's Middle Ages, and copy them. The screen may be his tribute to them, and Sesson's own restless, mysterious waves may have set it off. Yet it is also very like one part of a screen by the painter Sōtatsu, in which a dragon climbs out of a stormy sea.
Another painter, Hōitsu, liked it enough to make a close copy, now in Tokyo. He swapped Kōrin's gold for a ground of silver leaf.

details.text: Look at the crests. The foam breaks into long hooked fingers, and some have small round holes punched clean through, with dark blue-green water showing behind.

Now look inside a wave. Its body is filled with close, sweeping lines running side by side, often in pairs. Kōrin probably drew them the old Chinese way, a pair of brushes gripped together in one fist, and the doubled strokes give the water its bulk.

At the right edge, a short column of writing ends in a round seal. The signature reads Hokkyō Kōrin; the seal reads Dōsū, a name he only began using in 1704. So the screen can be no earlier than that year.

context.text: Two moments from Genesis share one small panel: on the left the world is being made, and on the right Adam and Eve are already being pushed out of the garden. Giovanni di Paolo is thought to have painted it for a many-panelled altarpiece in the church of San Domenico in Siena, now called the Guelfi Altarpiece. That altarpiece was taken apart and scattered long ago. Several big panels are in the Uffizi in Florence. The Met owns this one and a compact Paradise with saints and angels.

The case for placing the panel in that altarpiece starts from an old description. In the seventeenth century, someone listed three subjects for the altarpiece's predella: the Creation of the World, the Last Judgment and the Flood. On that basis one reconstruction adds two more scenes, Paradise and Hell, to make a predella of five, with this Creation and Expulsion among them. The link is hypothetical, though it may be right. Judged by style, this panel and the Met's Paradise may both date from around 1445.

One later owner was Camille Benoît, a French composer who was also a curator at the Louvre. The Kleinberger gallery's inventory card called the picture Paradise Lost, a nod to Milton's epic. In January 1917 Kleinberger sold it to Philip Lehman, an American banker, for $9,000. Battle was raging across Europe, and a note on the stock card warned that the painting was "to be delivered after the war." It reached the Met in 1975 with the Robert Lehman Collection.

details.text: Look at the great disc God is pointing at. It stands for the Creation of the World of the title. Ring inside ring, it narrows to a round patch of brown mountains and green ground at the very centre, while God's finger points down at its outer rim.

Now look right. The angel expelling Adam and Eve is as naked as they are, marked out only by gold wings and a gold halo. It lays a hand on Adam's shoulder and pushes. Adam turns back toward the angel even as he reaches for Eve, who is already walking away.

context.text: The goldsmith once wore a halo that Petrus Christus never painted. It turned out to be a later addition and was taken off in 1993. Who he is remains unclear. He may be Saint Eligius, patron saint of goldsmiths, who mattered especially in Bruges, where he was linked with several craft guilds, goldsmiths among them. Or he may be a well-known goldsmith of Christus's own time. Saints in early Netherlandish pictures seldom had halos anyway.

On its face the scene is simple: a well-dressed couple picks out a ring while the goldsmith weighs it on a hand balance. Yet the figures are life-size, which is highly unusual. One persuasive explanation is that this is a portrait of a trade, painted to commemorate it, and perhaps to hang in a guild chapel. That would fit the care spent on the goldsmith's face, more individual than his customers', and the fact that his figure carries the most underdrawing. Beyond who painted it and when, very little about the picture is certain.

In 1815 the picture was sold at Frankfurt as a work by Jan van Eyck. It passed through German collections, among them the Oppenheims' in Cologne, reached Philip Lehman in New York in 1920, and came to the Met with the Robert Lehman Collection in 1975. Yet Christus had signed it plainly along the bottom edge: "Master Petrus Christus made me in the year 1449." After the date comes a small mark that appears to be a heart joined to parts of a clock mechanism. He used it on no other painting.

details.text: Look at the round mirror propped on the right end of the counter, against the post of the stall. It turns the room around: in it you see a street of gabled houses under a pale sky, and two men, one holding a falcon. Goldsmiths often kept convex mirrors to watch for thieves. Here it may also carry a moral. A falconer would have been an odd sight in a Bruges street. One reading takes the falcon as a sign of pride and greed, set against the solemn couple inside. Another sees the pair simply as idle young bachelors, the falcon a badge of the leisure class.

The shelves are not just stock. Next to the beads, brooches and rings are things people believed could ward off harm: the red branch of coral, fossil shark's teeth, a cup made from a coconut shell. On the lower shelf at the right stands a crystal vessel with a domed gold lid, perhaps made to hold a relic or the wafers of the Mass.

Follow the balance. Its pans tip toward the couple, which may hint at their future faithfulness, or at the Last Judgment. Now look at the counter on the left, where a red band lies coiled. One reading takes it for a bridal girdle, placed there to stress that this is a marriage, set against the idle pair in the mirror.

context.text: The painter set us high above Golgotha, the hill of the Crucifixion. From up there the land opens out into a wide landscape with room for several moments of the Passion at once, each on its own stretch of hillside. Close to us are Mary Magdalene, the Virgin, John and Saint Veronica with her cloth. On the right ride Longinus and the centurion.

Jacob Cornelisz van Oostsanen, also called Jacob van Amsterdam, came from a family of artists and was its best-known member. The panel is dated c. 1507–10, but its oak planks tell a more complicated story. The youngest growth ring formed in 1486, so the wood could have been ready by 1497, yet the likelier date for the painting is 1511 or later.

It came to the museum from a sale in 's-Hertogenbosch in 1901, bought with help from the Vereniging Rembrandt. Apart from a heavily discoloured varnish and a few retouchings along the plank joins that have changed colour, it survives in good condition.

details.text: Read the hills from the far left. Up in the corner, below a rock, Christ kneels to pray in Gethsemane, an angel with a cross on the rock above him and three figures asleep below. Lower down, he takes leave of his mother. Across on the right, he carries the cross among soldiers.

Now drop to the lower right corner. Saint Veronica kneels there, holding up her cloth with Christ's face printed on it. Gold letters on the border of her robe read ‘SALVE SANCT[A] FACIES NOS[TRI] REDEMTOR’.

context.text: The Israelites had turned away from God to worship a golden calf. Few painters took on that story, and Lucas van Leyden staged it in one landscape that runs straight through all three panels. It is a warning against unfaithfulness and dissolute living. Why did Lucas choose so rare a subject? Perhaps because Protestantism was growing, and Protestants deeply opposed the Catholic veneration of sacred images.

Lucas, a painter of Leiden, made it around 1530; another account puts it about 1525–30. Behind the Israelite camp, drawn in loving detail, rises a dramatic landscape. The scalloped top fits its time: early in the sixteenth century, Northern artists liked such inventive shapes for small triptychs.

It was recorded in a house on the Kalverstraat in Amsterdam in 1604. It sold in Paris in 1870, and the Rijksmuseum bought it from a Paris estate in June 1952. Long before either, in May 1709, it had fetched 1,470 guilders at an Amsterdam sale, listed as Lucas van Leyden's dancers round the golden calf, with a crowd of figures, in a handsome case.

details.text: Look for the calf itself. It is a small gold figure on top of a tall column, halfway back in the centre panel. Israelites dance around it, some hand in hand, and a band of musicians plays at its left. Far behind, Moses is on Mount Sinai.

Yet the idol is small and set far back. The foreground belongs to the feast instead: whole families sit on the ground with their children, eating and drinking. The celebration carries on into both wings, and at the left of the right wing a couple embrace.

context.text: Philip became Duke of Burgundy at four. His mother, Mary, Duchess of Burgundy, died in 1482 and the title passed to her small son, though he only began to rule in his own right in 1494. His father was the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I. In 1496 Philip married Joan the Mad, who stood to inherit Castile and Aragon.

Several related portraits of the young ruler survive, some of them fairly distant copies. Their general resemblance suggests they go back to one official likeness, and the closest to this one is at Windsor Castle. In the entrance room of her palace at Mechelen, Margaret of Austria displayed official portraits of the Burgundian court, among them a small one of Philip in a fur-lined gold brocade gown. It need not have been this panel.

Who painted it is unknown. It was once given to Philip's court painter Jacob van Laethem, and also to the Master of the Magdalen Legend; both attributions have since been rejected. Philip's other court painter, Pieter van Coninxloo, has been suggested for a related version in Brussels. It is dated about 1500, though tree-ring dating of the panel allows use from 1487 and favours 1501 or later.

details.text: Look at the patterned collar round his neck. From it hangs a small golden ram's fleece, the Golden Fleece order's badge. Only the greatest nobles and princes could belong.
Look at the cap. Pinned to its front is a gold medallion with two angels crowning the Virgin Mary. Infrared images show the cap itself was first planned smaller.

context.text: Anthony made his home in the desert, and his legend says the demons never left him alone there. They came as monsters and as naked women. He lived from 251 to about 356 and is generally held to have founded monasticism.

Bosch put his signature at bottom left of the middle panel. He made earth, water, air and fire into a stage for horrible beings: a crush of creatures, some real and some invented, standing for the fears and temptations that dog every human step.
