The inside shows three episodes of Anthony's legend: tempted and led astray by demons, he finds his way toward salvation in the hermit's life. The life of contemplation is held up as the ideal in an evil world. Bosch painted it around 1500, in the years of his great triptychs.

Most of the time the wings stood closed. Their outer faces show, in monochrome, ordinary people harassing Christ on the road to Calvary, under a moonlit gloom. The triptych's recorded history begins in 1913, at Lisbon's Necessidades Palace. When Lisbon lent it to the Prado in 2016, Madrid lent back Dürer's 1498 self-portrait.

details.text: Look at the kneeling saint at the centre. A woman in a white headdress leans over him with a bowl, but his eyes are on you: he looks straight out of the picture and lifts a hand, a gesture read as a blessing. Further back, in a dark doorway, Christ stands beside a crucifix on an altar and watches.
The left wing tells his ordeal twice. High in the sky, demons haul him through the air. Lower down, two monks and a layman help the half-dead hermit home along a plank walkway, after his flight.
In the right wing Anthony sits apart over an open book, praying. Across from him, at the left of the wing, a pale naked woman waits inside a hollow tree trunk. He keeps his eyes off her.

context.text: The giant is dead, his head in the boy's fist, and David is not celebrating. His face is turned up, lips parted. He is thanking God. Pictures of David usually show the victor showing off; as a way of painting him, this quiet one is extremely rare.

Lodovico Fermi of Piacenza acquired it from the painter in October 1650, and Guercino's studio account book for that year lists it as a David holding Goliath's head made for Fermi. By 1680 it had passed to Ranuccio Farnese II, Duke of Parma. Two copies by Guercino's students still exist. The picture had admirers from the day it was painted.

details.text: Look past him at the sky. Behind the upturned face is a darkened form of lapis lazuli, a pigment long tied to heaven and to God. Guercino favoured this deep blue in these years.

Now compare his two hands. One lies flat on his chest; the other still grips the giant's head by the hair, on a block of stone. Thanks and victory share one pose. Even the plumed red cap is off, hung on the sword hilt at left.

context.text: The Temeraire had helped defend Nelson's flagship Victory at Trafalgar in 1805, and was known ever after as the Fighting Temeraire. By 1838 she was over forty years old and worth only her timbers. In September that year she was towed from Sheerness up the Thames to Rotherhithe, to be scrapped.

It is unlikely that Turner saw the tow; he recreated it from reports, though one account says he came upon the ship on a Thames excursion. He kept the picture until he died in 1851, calling it 'his Darling'. A would-be buyer reputedly offered £5,000, and then a blank cheque, and was refused.
When it went on show at the Academy in 1839, Turner attached lines adapted from a poem: 'The flag which braved the battle and the breeze, / No longer owns her.'

details.text: Turner bent the facts. The real ship had been stripped of her masts; he gives her three, and repaints her black and yellow hull a ghostly white and gold.
He also moved the tug's black funnel to stand in front of its mast, so the sooty smoke streams back through the old ship's rigging. When an engraver later 'corrected' the tug, Turner was furious.
And the sun sets in the wrong place. A ship coming up the Thames was heading west, so the sunset could not have been behind it.
X-rays reveal a big sail painted where the tug and its smoking funnel now stand: Turner seems to have reused a canvas on which he had begun a sailing boat.

context.text: In December 1910 Marc wrote to August Macke about colour. Blue, he said, stood for the male principle and yellow for the female; red stood for matter. This picture puts that theory on show more plainly than almost any other.

The blue has nothing to do with real horses: Marc is painting what he saw as the essence of the animal, not its outward look. The foal became one of the most famous images of Marc and of the Blue Rider, the Munich circle whose first exhibition opened in the winter of 1911.

It came to the Lenbachhaus in 1965 through a foundation in the name of Bernhard and Elly Koehler. Bernhard Koehler, a rich Berlin industrialist, had bought the circle's work and helped pay for its exhibitions.

details.text: The foal faces us squarely, head bent and turned aside, as if deep in thought.
Marc sets colours against each other: red against green on the ground, cool blue and violet hills against warm yellow.

context.text: In October 1767 the painter Gabriel-François Doyen told the playwright Charles Collé about an odd request. A gentleman, pointing to his mistress, wanted her painted on a swing pushed by a bishop, with himself placed where he could see her legs. Doyen, stunned, sent him on to Fragonard, who took the job; by the time Collé wrote, Fragonard was already at work.

Collé never names the patron. He is usually taken to be a very rich tax farmer for the French clergy, which might explain the wish for a bishop. In the finished picture no bishop pushes the swing: an elderly husband works the ropes, while her young lover lies among the bushes below.

Swings were hugely popular at the time, and not only for fun. Long prescribed for the sick, by the 18th century they were even tried as a cure for melancholy, seasickness and impotence, and were often found in brothels.
By 1865, when the 4th Marquess of Hertford bought it at a Paris sale, it ranked among France's best-known pictures. Six years before, the Louvre had been offered it, and said no.

details.text: Up goes the swing and off flies a slipper, leaving the young man below with a view meant for him alone. He raises his hat toward her, a hint of his delight.
The little statue at the left is Falconet's Menacing Cupid, made for Madame de Pompadour, the mistress of Louis XV.
Swirling diagonals and bright pink set against blue-green come from the style of Fragonard's teacher, François Boucher.

Cleaning in 2021 found little underdrawing: Fragonard seems to have painted straight onto the canvas. It also revealed changes he made as he went, to the woman's knee and petticoat and to the young man's right shoulder.

context.text: In the Spanish town of Monforte de Lemos, this Netherlandish altarpiece once passed for a Rubens. The Jesuits of Monforte credited it to him, and its colour helps explain the mistake: glowing crimson and red set against warm browns and greens. Its real painter was Hugo van der Goes. Berlin bought it from the monastery at Monforte in 1914, and it still carries the town's name.

Parts of it look Italian, too. Cut out on their own, the portrait-like heads at the back could be mistaken for Florentine work. That fed an old idea, first put forward in 1859, that Hugo travelled to Italy before joining the painters' guild in 1467. Against that, it has been argued that an Italian look need not mean he ever went there.
Where it falls in his career is disputed too. Berlin dates it about 1470–1475. One view puts it four or five years before his Portinari triptych; another places it after that altarpiece.

What survives is only the middle of something much bigger. This was the centre of a large triptych, and the old frame still has iron hinges on its sides where the movable wings hung. Both wings are gone. Copies show a Nativity on the left and the Circumcision on the right. Opened out, the whole altarpiece was nearly six metres wide.

details.text: Look at the very top, in the raised middle section. The purple and golden-yellow cloth hanging there belongs to angels who once hovered over the scene. The top of the panel was cut down, so only the lower parts of their robes are left.

The eldest king kneels before the child, hands joined in prayer. On the floor beside his gift on the rock lies his fur hat ringed with a jewelled crown, taken off as a sign of humility. The three kings are clearly of different ages: young, middle-aged and old. That was a motif from the 1300s, read as an allusion to the three ages of man bowing before Christ.

Now find the shepherds, small and far off through the opening at the top, just right of centre, among their sheep. In a fourteenth-century legend they told the kings of the miracle they had seen and pointed the way. And at the lower left, beside Joseph, grow blue irises, a quiet hint of the Passion that is easy to overlook.

context.text: The Annunciation at the centre was probably not made to order at all. It reuses a slightly earlier design from Robert Campin's workshop in Tournai, and seems to have been painted first. Soon afterwards a buyer ordered the two wings, apparently from two different painters, and had himself put in the left one. Later still, in the 1430s and presumably after he married, his wife and the messenger at the gate were painted in. Infrared and X-ray images show the left wing first existed without them.

Even the windows changed. The central panel's windows were first covered in gold leaf, then painted over with blue sky and coats of arms. The shield in the left window was traced in 1898 to a Mechelen family whose name appears as Ymbrechts, Ingelbrechts, Engelbrechts and more; the right-hand shield has been tied, less convincingly, to a family from Düsseldorf. One elaborate theory points to a thrice-married Peter Engelbrechts, with ties to both Cologne and Mechelen. The oak boards tell a similar story: the centre's timber may have been cut as much as twenty-five years before the wings' timber, a hint, though not proof, that the parts were painted at different times.

Who held the brush is unsettled too. Campin, sometimes called the Master of Flémalle, is documented with at least two assistants, among them the young Rogier van der Weyden, who worked in his shop from 1427 to 1432. The triptych is credited to Campin's workshop, about 1427–32; it has also been given to Campin and an assistant, possibly Rogier, about 1425–30. Whoever painted it, its owners would have prayed before it at home, and a conception of Christ in a room much like their own may have fed their hope of children. The wife kneels behind her husband, unable to see into the room, so she can only picture the miracle in her mind.

details.text: Look at the round window above the angel's wings. Sliding down the golden rays is a tiny figure holding a cross: the Christ Child, arriving in person. This homely, rather undignified way of showing the conception drew objections from theologians from the start, and a pope later condemned it.

Now look at the table. A thin thread of smoke rises from the candle, the pages of the open book are lifting, and a scroll has rolled loose beside it. The sudden arrival from the left seems to have just put the flame out. One reading is that the lilies in the jug sit so naturally on the table that, without other Annunciations to go by, nobody would take them for more than a pleasant still life. Putting the Annunciation in a home, rather than a church or its doorway, was a striking novelty at the time.

On the right, Joseph, Mary's betrothed, is boring holes in a board. On his bench sits a small half-made box device, and another stands finished on the ledge outside his window. They are mousetraps, and they are thought to allude to Saint Augustine, who called the cross the Devil's mousetrap with Christ as the bait. The board itself has been read three ways: the lid of a bait box, a strainer for a winepress, or a fire screen. Nobody is sure.

context.text: Manet sent just this one picture to the Salon of 1875, hoping not to be turned away. It was let in, and once again his work drew violent attacks. It was not a popular picture.

It began with an invitation. In the summer of 1874 Monet asked his friend to come and paint with him, to catch the light forever shifting on the water. Manet stayed several weeks on family property at Gennevilliers, across the Seine from Argenteuil. Watching Monet paint at Argenteuil won him over to working out of doors. His colours grew brighter and his touch smaller.

Manet would never part with it. Only in 1889, after his death, could the collector Henri Van Cutsem buy it from his widow, Suzanne. He later left his collection to the city of Tournai, whose museum now holds the only two Manets in Belgium.

details.text: Look straight down from the far chimney. A short line seems to drop from it into the river, like a reflection. It is not one. At the top are two rope ends hanging from the tip of the furled sail; below them, a few small yellow flowers come loose from the band of the woman's hat.
The boatman turning toward her has the features of Rudolf Leenhoff, Manet's brother-in-law. The woman's identity remains unknown. She faces straight out at us, not at him.

context.text: Why paint a flower this big? O'Keeffe remembered admiring a small flower still life by Fantin-Latour while skyscrapers seemed to go up overnight in New York. Painted that small, she reasoned, her flowers would go unseen, because she was unknown. “So I thought I'll make them look big like the huge buildings going up. People will be startled; they'll have to look at them—and they did.”

The giant flowers startled even the man closest to her. Alfred Stieglitz, her husband and her dealer, was shocked by how bold they were when the first of them went on show in 1924. This one was exhibited in 1927 as The Dark Iris No. III.

From the mid-1920s critics read her flowers as sexual metaphors. She denied it again and again: “you hung all your own associations with flowers on my flower and you write about my flower as if I think and see what you think and see of the flower—and I don't.” The argument has never been settled.
She owned it until 1969. By the time she gave it to the Met, it had already hung there on loan for twenty years. In 1973 one publication even printed it upside down.

details.text: Nothing here is life size. Seen this close, the petals turn into soft shifts from white to grey and ruffled edges you would never stop to notice in a garden.
Look into the heart of the flower: grey-violet folds darken to near black, split down the middle by a thin seam of dark red.

context.text: Until recently, most people assumed Potter had painted a real animal. He could not have. The horns and the loose fold of skin under the throat belong to a bull of about two, yet the mouth holds the six big adult teeth of one aged three or four, and the perspective does not hold together. Potter must have assembled his bull from sketches of several different animals.

He was 22 when he signed it in 1647. Nobody is known to have painted anything as everyday as a bull at such a size before: about 2.4 metres high and 3.4 wide. Most of his pictures were small scenes of country life, and why he made this one so big is a mystery.

It made him famous. In 1795 French troops took it to Paris with some two hundred other works from the gallery of William V in The Hague; in the Louvre it hung among the Raphaels and Titians Napoleon had seized in Italy. It was back in The Hague by 1816 and moved to the Mauritshuis in 1822. In the early nineteenth century this bull was what brought visitors from far and wide, and it counted among the best-known Dutch paintings of all.

details.text: Look at the farmer, the sheep and the distant meadow: they were added later. Seams still visible in the canvas show that Potter first meant to paint the bull alone. He then attached strips of linen 40 to 60 cm wide down both sides and along the top, and painted the rest on them. A farm scene with more animals and a farmer was surely more appealing to buyers than a lone bull.

Now look closer. Flies have settled on the white patch across the bull's back. One of the sheep lying at left has just been shorn, and the shears have left their marks in its fleece. Far off, above the trees on the right, rises the spire of Rijswijk's church.

The farmer stands by the tree with one hand on its trunk, in a ragged hat and torn clothes. Many Dutch viewers know his face: he served as the model for Teun, a character in children's first reading books. Potter signed and dated the fence rail beside him. The precision that once made the picture a sensation has worn less well since: to later taste it can look dry and laboured.

context.text: In 1830 Delacroix's career had stalled: his Death of Sardanapalus had failed badly in 1828, and nobody bought it. Then, during the 'three glorious days' of 27–29 July 1830, he watched Parisians rise up to defend the nation's sovereignty and individual liberty, and saw the tricolour return after fifteen years of censorship.

He set to work in September, swept along by joy, and finished in December, in barely four months. It is at once a history painting and an allegory, with scenes of daily life, portraits, still life and a view of the city. The French state bought it in 1831 for 3,000 francs.
It is his most famous painting, yet untypical: the only time he painted Paris, and the only large canvas he gave to the working people of his own country and time.

details.text: The heart of the picture is a pyramid: the barricade as its base, Liberty as its centre of gravity, and the tricolour as its crown.
The boy with pistols, often nicknamed Gavroche though Hugo's character came much later, runs ahead of Liberty, not beside her.

The restoration of 2023–24 brought a surprise: Liberty's tunic, thought to be wholly yellow, was first painted light grey. Delacroix added bright yellow over it, dense at the bust and thinner further down the legs.
In the bottom left corner lies a worn leather shoe, abandoned in the rubble. Even the curator had not noticed it before the cleaning.

context.text: Who is he? There have been fresh attempts to identify the wanderer, but nothing reliable tells us whom Friedrich might have been portraying.

His clothes show that he is a city dweller who has gone out into nature to enjoy it. He has reached the peak and pauses at the view. Yet we look less at the view than over his shoulder, and seeing itself can be read as the real subject.
Figures seen from behind became Friedrich's way of picturing a personal experience of nature; faceless, they can stand for everyone. The picture is dated about 1817, or by another account about 1818.

details.text: The rock he stands on comes from a drawing Friedrich made on the Kaiserkrone, a peak in Saxon Switzerland he climbed on 3 June 1813.
The cone-shaped mountain on the left comes from an 1808 study of the Rosenberg in Bohemian Switzerland. It answers the distinctive Zirkelstein on the right.
The man stands at the middle of the picture, and the slopes on either side run down towards him.

context.text: Ingres grumbled about the endless requests for 'wretched portraits' that kept him from history painting. At first he refused this one. Then he met the sitter, 23-year-old Inès Moitessier, wife of the wealthy Sigisbert Moitessier, and called her 'beautiful and good'.

That was 1844. The portrait took twelve years. His wife's death in 1849 left him unable to paint for months. In 1851 he gave up and painted a quite different, standing Madame Moitessier in black, now in Washington, then came back to this one.

Along the way the picture went through several major revisions. Her little daughter Catherine was meant to lean against her mother's knees, but could not keep still, and Ingres took her out of the composition. The dress went from dark, to yellow, and finally, in 1855, to the fashionable flowered silk from Lyon she wears now.
Picasso saw the picture in 1921 and never forgot it. Eleven years later he borrowed her hand at the temple for his own Woman with a Book.

details.text: Her pose, head resting on a finger, comes from an ancient wall painting found at Herculaneum. The figure is identified as the goddess of Arcadia, though when found it was known as Flora. Ingres probably saw it in Naples in 1814.

Look in the mirror. Her reflection does not quite match her pose. The little cupid on the sofa's carving has no reflection, though the carving does. Perhaps Ingres was bending space on purpose; perhaps it is because he did not paint her in that room.
The crinoline was brand new, introduced only the year before, and spreads the silk out for display. So was the hairstyle, pulled back to show a provocative glimpse of the ear.
Read the signature. It gives not the sitter's age but the painter's: 76.

context.text: The story is one of slow recognition, but Caravaggio paints the instant it breaks. The two disciples at the table realise who their companion is: one is about to spring from his chair, the other flings out his arms in disbelief.

Caravaggio painted it in 1601 for Ciriaco Mattei, after his paintings of Saint Matthew in San Luigi dei Francesi had caused a sensation. Mattei paid 150 scudi in January 1602, a high price: that year a church offered Caravaggio only 40 for an altarpiece.
It soon passed to the Borghese collection in Rome, likely first to Cardinal Scipione Borghese, and stayed there until the early 1800s. It was given to the National Gallery in 1839.

details.text: The innkeeper stands outside the moment, thumbs in his belt, his face partly in shadow. He has not yet 'seen the light'.
Light streams in from the left onto Christ and the disciple at right, often identified as Saint Peter. It throws a shadow on the wall behind Christ, almost a reverse halo.
The basket of fruit teeters on the very edge of the table. Its shadow on the white cloth has been read as the shape of a fish, another sign of Christ.
The disciple at right wears a scallop shell, the badge of a pilgrim. And at the near side of the table, a place is left empty, as if for us.

context.text: Ensor pictured Christ arriving in modern Brussels in the middle of a Mardi Gras parade. The haloed figure at the centre is partly Ensor himself: a lonely visionary whom the crowd barely notices.
It was long said that Ensor's own artists' group, Les XX, rejected the picture. More likely it simply was not finished in time, and it was never sent.

Either way, it stayed in his studio, too big for any wall to hold, until he moved in 1917 into a house he had inherited. Apart from two retrospectives, in 1929 and 1939, it was seen only by visitors to his home.
After Ensor died it hung for a time in the casino at Knokke, where gamblers could add themselves to the painted crowd. In 1987 Belgium waived its right to buy it, and the Getty Museum did.

details.text: Look for Christ: a small figure with a yellow halo, in the middle of the parade. A triangle of chrome yellow once made him stand out, but the paint has faded.
The banner overhead reads “Vive la Sociale”, “Long live the social”. One reading is that the odd phrase, rather than naming socialism, muddles any political message.

Ensor laid the paint on with palette knives and spatulas and scratched it with the end of his brush. He claimed it was common house paint; analysis at the Getty found ordinary artists' pigments of the time.

context.text: Piero painted this for his family's house in Borgo San Sepolcro, where it hung at first in the main bedroom. It stayed with the family until 1825. Likely painted in the early 1480s, it was among his last works, though another account dates it 1470–75.

While it was still in the family, overcleaning badly damaged parts of the paint, and some came to believe it unfinished. A restoration completed in 2022 recovered much of Piero's intention: the sense of space, the holy light falling on the stable, and the deliberate absence of shadows under the figures.
He set the Nativity on a hilltop near his hometown, as a miraculous vision, following the famous account of the 14th-century mystic Saint Bridget of Sweden.

details.text: Mary kneels before her son. She has spread out her deep blue cloak, her only possession, to keep his bare skin off the ground.
Five wingless angels in loose, draped clothes that recall ancient sculpture sing and play, a heavenly accompaniment to a rustic scene.
Joseph sits on a saddle, posed like a famous ancient statue of a boy pulling a thorn from his foot. One writer calls showing the sole of his foot an unprecedentedly indecorous pose.
One shepherd looks out at us and points up towards a hole in the shed's roof, where the divine light falls. Look also for the magpie on the roof, and finches among the rocks in front.

context.text: For nearly 250 years the Sistine Madonna was scarcely known outside its church in Piacenza. Pope Julius II had almost certainly commissioned it for the high altar of San Sisto there, probably after Piacenza joined the Papal States in 1512. Only its acquisition for Dresden in 1752–54, after nearly two years of hard bargaining, brought it before the public.

From around 1800 it was copied in paintings and prints, and turned up in magazines, embroidery, advertisements, caricatures and scrapbooks. The two little angels at the bottom were lifted out on their own and began a solo career.

After the Second World War it was taken to Russia, and a legend spread that the Soviet army had rescued it. In 1955 it went to Berlin for an exhibition marking its return, and reached Dresden in 1956.

details.text: Raphael added the two little angels leaning on the ledge at the very end, mainly for the composition's sake.
The open curtain reveals a vision of the world beyond. Mary carries the Child out of the heavens to earth, a kind of image of his birth.
Look at the pale sky on either side, by the curtains: it is made of countless faint angel heads.

Saint Sixtus kneels humbly at the left, Saint Barbara at the right lost in thought; both were venerated at San Sisto's high altar. The serious faces of mother and child seem to know the Passion to come.

context.text: Asked for a title for the catalogue of the 1874 exhibition, Monet balked at calling it a view of Le Havre and told them to put “Impression”. The word was already painters' jargon for capturing an atmosphere rather than describing nature in detail.

The conservative critic Louis Leroy, covering the show for a satirical paper, seized on the title for a ferocious article on 'the impressionists'. 'Wallpaper in its embryonic state,' one of his characters scoffs, 'is more finished than that seascape.' A few days later Jules Castagnary took up the word in praise, and it stuck to Monet and his friends.
The picture became the emblem of the group. It came to the Musée Marmottan in 1940, a gift from Eugène and Victorine Donop de Monchy.

details.text: Monet painted the view from his hotel window in Le Havre, around November 1872, looking over the outer harbour in the early morning.
He painted it in a few hours. The ferrymen's boats in front, the bright orange sun and its reflections were added as he finished.
Behind, cranes, chimneys and masts dissolve in the mist of an autumn dawn.

context.text: In 1700 the King of Spain, Charles II, died without children, having named Louis XIV's grandson Philippe d'Anjou as his heir. Louis had Rigaud paint the new King of Spain. Philippe, for his part, wanted to take a portrait of his grandfather with him to Madrid, by the same hand.

The result was too admired to give away. Louis kept it, and Rigaud had to paint a second version for his grandson. One report at the time said the opposite: that the king would keep his promise and send the original.

This first version, the only one signed and dated, hung over the fireplace in the Salon d'Apollon, the throne room at Versailles. Seized at the Revolution, it came to the Louvre in 1814. The second version now hangs in that room instead.

details.text: Look at the leg thrust forward. Rigaud probably took the pose from a 1686 statue of the king trampling a Hydra, a many-headed monster. The monster has gone; now the leg seems to recall Louis's old passion for dance.

The regalia are not the ones you might expect. The sceptre he holds upside down is Henri IV's short one, not Charlemagne's. Beside it on the cushion lie the hand of justice, a small hand on a rod, and a crown that is not Charlemagne's either, but a lighter silver-gilt one made for royal funerals.
Rigaud signed the picture twice: on the ribbon above the relief of Justice on the column base, and more discreetly where the carpet meets the robe.

context.text: Five women sit on the sofas and wait. No two of them meet each other's eyes, and nobody seems to be talking. In front, one has hitched her white shift up over a dark green stocking and holds her leg; the woman beside her, in pink, keeps her eyes down. Behind them, the two women at the left both look away to the right, and the woman at the back stares out.

Lautrec knew such rooms from the inside. He sometimes stayed in brothels for weeks, and the women there came to treat him as a friend. What he painted was the dull sameness of their working days: the long wait for clients, the medical checks they were made to undergo.

Albi owns two pictures with this title, one in oil on canvas and one in oil on cardboard. Both entered the museum in 1922, the year his mother gave Albi, the city where he was born, a large collection of his work. The museum dates the canvas to 1894. Which of the two this image shows is not certain.

details.text: Look at the faces. Each is drawn as a different person: the sharp profile at far left, the heavy, pale face at the back, the downcast eyes of the woman in pink. Yet several of the women share the same orange-red hair, piled up high, and the same pale skin.

Now look at the lower half. A wide mauve sofa fills the lower left corner, and nobody is sitting on it. At the right edge the only woman on her feet has her back to us, and the frame cuts her in half. Where she is going, the picture does not say.

context.text: He holds a halberd, part spear and part battle-axe, and stares straight out with a soldier's swagger. Yet his body is slight and his face has no lines at all: he can be no more than a teenager. Behind him rise flat, angled planes of green, standing, it seems, for one of the city's bastions. The picture bears no signature and no date, and is placed around 1529–30.

Who he is remains open to debate. He may be Francesco Guardi. Vasari wrote that during the siege of Florence Pontormo made a very beautiful portrait of Guardi dressed as a soldier. Vasari added that Bronzino later painted a cover for it, showing Pygmalion praying to Venus. This may be that portrait. A birth record does survive for a boy named Francesco born into the Guardi family in 1514. But a 1612 inventory of the Riccardi family in Florence has led some to propose a different sitter: Cosimo de' Medici himself.

The painter's name drifted too. Past owners recorded the picture as the work of Gianfrancesco Penni, of Andrea del Sarto and of Bronzino. It passed through the Riccardi family by inheritance and through a Paris sale in 1810. In 1989 the Getty bought it at Christie's in New York.

details.text: Look at the left hand pushed into his hip. It repeats the pose of two famous Florentine statues of David, by Donatello and by Verrocchio, both symbols of the city. He is smartly dressed, in a silk jacket and red breeches, with a sword at his side.
Now look at the small gold plaque hanging from links at the side of his red cap. It shows Hercules struggling with Antaeus.

context.text: Holbein spent years away in England. Back in Basel between trips, in 1528 or 1529, he painted his wife Elsbeth with their two eldest children, Philipp and Katharina.
Elsbeth was left for long stretches to raise their children alone. All three faces look sad, and people have tried to explain why, from a deserted wife's grief to sore, inflamed eyes.

Holbein went back to England without it. Even before his death Elsbeth had let it go: by 1542 the Zurich painter Hans Asper had it. Copies made mostly in the 16th century show how soon it became famous; one, in Lille, is titled Caritas, or Charity.

details.text: Mother and children make a pyramid, like the old pictures of Saint Anne with her daughter Mary and the Christ Child, or of Mary with the infant Jesus and John. Her hand on the boy's shoulder recalls Leonardo, whose work Holbein probably saw in France in 1524.
Yet this pyramid will not settle. The girl gazes off to the right and the boy looks up the same way, toward someone who may once have stood there: perhaps Holbein himself, at his easel.

Holbein painted on paper. At some point the figures were cut out round their outlines, the sheet apparently trimmed hard at two sides, and the whole glued to a dark panel. The date at lower right lost its last digit in the process.

context.text: While Moses was up on Mount Sinai collecting the Ten Commandments, his people chose another god. Aaron, the man in the white cloak, melted down their gold earrings to make the idol they now dance around.
The Bible calls it a calf, but this is a bull. Poussin probably meant Apis, the bull-god of Egypt, so the Israelites are slipping back into Egyptian ritual.

Poussin painted it in 1633–34 for Amedeo dal Pozzo's palace in Turin, with a companion piece, The Crossing of the Red Sea. Around 1680 it was apparently sold to a painter buying for Louis XIV. The pair stayed together until 1945; the companion is now in Melbourne.
Centuries later the picture was the target of a deliberate attack, and in 1978 it had to be repaired and retouched.

details.text: Look at the top left. Moses is back, Joshua at his side. Furious at what he sees, he lifts the stone tablets to smash them.

The dancers' muscular bodies and flowing robes come from Poussin's study of ancient sculpture. Turned the other way round, the same group already appears in his earlier picture of a pagan revel. He is said to have posed little clay figures as models.
Exodus says the people were naked. Poussin chose not to show them so: apart from the small children, his crowd is draped.
On the right, tents show that the worshippers have travelled far. A bright light falls from our side; an old man standing before the tents raises a hand to shade his eyes.

context.text: Carpaccio puts the miracle off to one side. Up in a loggia over the Grand Canal, the patriarch of Grado, Francesco Querini, holds a relic of the Holy Cross before a man possessed by a spirit, and the man is cured on the spot. The rest of the canvas goes to Venice itself: its bridge, its boats and its noisy everyday life.

The relic had once belonged to the patriarch of Constantinople. In 1369 it came to the Venetian confraternity of San Giovanni Evangelista, a gift from Filippo de Mezières, Cyprus's grand chancellor. From the mid-1490s Carpaccio, Gentile Bellini and three other painters filled the room that kept it with scenes of its miracles. This one dates from about 1494–96. The wonders were set in real, recognisable places, such as Piazza San Marco or the Rialto, and painted exactly, so that they would be easier to believe.

Within half a century the canvas was cut. In 1544, probably to fit new doors, several paintings, this one among them, lost a strip from the bottom. The brothers took expert advice first. The record says "the very wise Master Titian" came to look, and that he recommended cutting some off the bottom, "saying the cut would not damage the said canvases in any way". A century later the picture was lengthened again by 27 centimetres, and the addition is plain to see.

details.text: Look at the bridge. This is the old wooden Rialto of 1458, and the painting is a rare record of it. Its middle section could be raised to let bigger ships through, and the ropes that lifted it are easy to pick out. In 1502 so many people crowded onto it that it almost collapsed. A new bridge, of stone, went up in 1591 and still stands.

Find the man in black in the loggia, head tipped back. A man in a white surplice and red cap holds a long gold staff with an ornate tip out toward him: this is the healing. To the right, white-hooded brothers kneel or hold tall gold candlesticks. The procession has climbed the steps to the loggia, where the patriarch, the city's spiritual leader, meets them.
Farther along the houses on the left, above a portico roof, a round sign hangs from an iron bracket. It marks an inn called the Sturgeon, and a real inn of that name once did business here.

context.text: Degas cared more about the hard work behind a performance than the performance itself. A friend in the orchestra got him backstage and into the dance studio of the old Paris Opéra, in the rue Le Peletier, before the new Garnier building replaced it.
He spent countless hours backstage there sketching, sometimes with the help of photographs, and built up a stock of poses. The finished compositions he put together back in his studio.

In 1876 he delivered this one to Deschamps in London, and it was shown in London and Brighton that year. Sold at Christie's in 1889, it was bought by Theo van Gogh, then working for the Paris dealers Goupil.

details.text: Class is almost over, and nobody is concentrating. One girl scratches her back; others stretch, or fix a ribbon, an earring, their hair. Right of centre, leaning on his stick, stands the stern old teacher, a portrait of a real ballet master, Jules Perrot. Hardly anyone is listening to him.

Degas looks down at a slant across the room, so the floorboards race away from us. The poet Paul Valéry wrote: “Degas is one of the very few painters who gave the ground its true importance. He has some admirable floors.”
Down at the lower left stands a green watering can, used to damp the dusty boards so the dancers would not slip. Degas signed his name on it.

context.text: Jupiter comes to Leda in the shape of a swan. Around 1532 Correggio painted a cycle of the god's love affairs, in his various disguises, for Federico II Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua. They have been counted among the most erotic pictures of the Renaissance, yet not one shows a man of flesh and blood.
Whom they were for is uncertain. Some were reportedly to be sent to the Emperor, and this canvas is said to have gone to Charles V; but the duke may have ordered the set for himself.

Its later life was violent. Swedish troops carried it off from Prague in 1648, and Queen Christina took it to Rome after giving up her throne. In France it came to Louis, son of the Regent, the Duke of Orléans. Offended by Leda, he cut the picture apart in a fit of religious frenzy.
The pieces were put back together and restored. Later it was bought on behalf of Frederick the Great, and by 1770 it hung in his picture gallery at Potsdam.

details.text: Look at Leda's face: it is not Correggio's. Her head was lost and repainted more than once, last in Berlin in 1834–35, when the scene's sensual pleasure was also toned down. At first she faced further to the right.
At the left a winged young Cupid plays a lyre, the instrument of divine music, and a small cupid below him blows a long horn.
Behind Leda, a maid in red lifts a white cloth over a bather climbing out of the water. At the far right, a swan swims up to a standing girl, and another hovers above the trees.

context.text: The chahut, or cancan, was a risqué dance: the women hitched up their skirts and kicked their legs in the air. The number is ending; legs fly up and hats are raised in salute to the audience.

It looks like a snapshot of Paris nightlife, but nothing here was quick. Seurat built it from countless tiny dots, lines and colour combinations, following a strict system; he said Charles Blanc's Grammar gave him the basis of his ideas about expressive line.

Shown at the Independents in 1890, it was widely discussed, but few praised it outright; many found its lines too schematic. In 1914 a German citizen offered it to the Louvre in vain, and in 1922 Mme Kröller-Müller bought it.

details.text: Almost every line in the picture climbs. Look at the kicking legs, the upturned moustaches and smiles, the scroll of the double bass, even the flower shapes on the wall. Seurat meant the rising lines to carry the excitement.
In the lower right corner a snub-nosed customer gazes up at the dancers: the leering male onlooker so often drawn in illustrations of such dances.
Around the edge runs a painted border of dots. It once worked with Seurat's frame, but a later owner had that frame replaced.

context.text: When a group of Modigliani's nudes went on show at Berthe Weill's gallery in Paris in 1917, the police stepped in. One account says they closed the exhibition, calling the pubic hair in some paintings obscene; another says they made Weill take the nudes down.

This picture stands at the very start of the development of his most celebrated group of nudes. It belongs to a series of female nudes he painted in 1916 and 1917, and her long face recalls sculpture from Egypt, Africa and Oceania, which Modigliani had studied in the Paris ethnographic museum.

Samuel Courtauld bought it by 1928 and gave it to the Courtauld in 1932. Its later history hints at how Modigliani showed such pictures: a photograph of 1959 shows an unvarnished strip along the lower edge, suggesting the nudes were displayed without varnish.

details.text: Her head drops onto her shoulder and her eyes are closed; her long dark hair falls behind her, with one lock over her chest.
Where is her right arm? Modigliani painted the blue background over it while it was still wet, to change the pose. That removed the arm as a distraction from the contrast between waist and hip.

Look closely at the hair on her head: deep lines are scratched into the wet paint, likely with a tool such as a brush-handle end or a knife tip. And of the nudes studied, only this one has curly pubic hair.

context.text: When Prince William V bought this panel at auction in Leiden in 1766, he paid 7,350 guilders, more than ten times the price of a painting by Van Dyck or Jordaens.

It is the work of two friends from the same town, Rubens and Brueghel, made as a showpiece of both men's skills. Brueghel planned the composition, but Rubens started it, sketching the two figures, the tree, the horse and the snake in thin paint. Brueghel then painted the plants and animals with encyclopaedic precision. Both signed it, though Rubens's share is far greater than the inscriptions suggest.
It is dated about 1615, or by another account about 1617. In 1795 the French confiscated it and carried it to Paris; it came back in 1815, and has hung in the Mauritshuis since 1822.

details.text: The serpent has given Eve the apple; now she passes it to Adam, who will soon eat the forbidden fruit.

Look behind Adam: a little monkey is biting into an apple, and a bird of paradise stands at his feet. In 1621 Brueghel wrote that he was watching and painting the creatures in Albert and Isabella's menagerie.

Brueghel worked over an underdrawing, but moved some things as he painted, like the yapping dogs in the middle of the garden. Rubens's figures show no underdrawing that can be seen: he painted the couple directly on the panel.

context.text: The legend tells of Ursula, a princess and a Christian, from Britain or perhaps Brittany, who went to Rome on pilgrimage with 11,000 virgins. Here her companions prepare to sail home. They carry bows and arrows, emblems of the martyrdom that awaits them: at Cologne, the legend says, the invading Huns killed them all.

Claude painted it in 1641 for Fausto Poli, who ran the household of Pope Urban VIII and looked after the Barberini family's property, shortly before he was made a cardinal. Claude lived most of his life in Rome, and the buildings echo ones he and Poli knew.

The story was popular in the 1500s but rarely painted in the 1600s. In the 20th century the legend itself was questioned, and Ursula's feast day of 21 October was removed from the Roman Catholic calendar.

details.text: The round temple at the left is based on the Tempietto at San Pietro in Montorio, built where Saint Peter was crucified. The museum likens the palace behind it to the home of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, the Pope's nephew.
Ursula, in yellow, holds up a white flag marked with a red cross as her companions file down the steps.
The ships in the centre fly blue flags; the museum identifies the emblem on them as that of the Barberini, Claude's most influential patrons.
As the museum points out, the prows of the moored ships on the right lead across to Ursula, and a pair of noblemen watching from the lower left corner steer our eyes to her too.

context.text: In 1912 Kandinsky went back to Moscow, the city where he was born. This painting was his answer to what he called "those . . . extremely powerful impressions I had experienced in Moscow—or more correctly, of Moscow itself." Over five months he worked through an oil sketch and at least ten other studies in watercolour, ink and pencil.

By 1913 he believed abstraction could reveal what lies hidden in the visible world. He also thought viewers needed time to follow him, so he kept fragments of real things in most of his work from these years. "We are still firmly bound to the outward appearance of nature and must draw forms from it," he wrote in his essay on this very painting.

details.text: At the upper left, three slanting black lines seem to stand for a troika, the Russian sleigh pulled by three horses. Another reading finds the troika in a three-lobed form nearby.

In the centre, the swirling blue mass has been read as St George on horseback, with a long pale lance pointing out to the left. An emblem of the saint was part of Peter the Great's state seal, so read this way the figure points to Moscow's tsarist past. Another reading sees the saint and the dragon as two separate forms joined by that glowing lance.
Kandinsky finally resolved the composition with the soft white border of the title, widest at the bottom and the right. He wrote elsewhere that white offers "the harmony of silence".

context.text: In the 1860s French painters and writers argued often about Wagner. Cézanne valued the composer too, and he thought about painting a picture called Ouverture du Tannhäuser. Fantin had already shown a scene from Tannhäuser at the Salon of 1864.

Cézanne painted this canvas at the Jas de Bouffan. When the dealer Ambroise Vollard acquired it in December 1899, it was listed simply as "Interior. Girl at the piano and girl sewing". It went to the Moscow collector Ivan Morozov in 1908 and reached the Hermitage in 1948.

details.text: At the left a young woman in a long white dress plays an upright piano, seen in profile with her eyes lowered to the keys. The overture of the title is Wagner's Tannhäuser, first played in Paris in 1860.
Further back, at the centre, a second woman in a dark shawl sits on a red sofa, sewing. They may be Cézanne's sisters, Marie and Rose, but the picture names no one.
Cézanne painted the subject three times, and this is the only version that survives.

context.text: Van Dyck's list of pictures for the king asked £200 for "the king at the hunt". The figure was struck out and £100 written beside it, halving the price. That item, paid for in 1638, has been identified with this picture, though the match has sometimes been doubted.

It has been read as showing the king as he would have wished to be remembered: elegant, cultured and needing no trappings to look like a ruler. Charles probably commissioned it, but he did not keep it: it is recorded in none of his palaces, so he may have given it to someone close to the court. It ended up in France, where Louis XVI acquired it in 1775.

details.text: The king has just got down from his horse after a hard ride. The pink garment at the centre of the picture, held by the young man, is the king's own, probably a coat he has just taken off.

Charles was an exceptionally small man, but you would not guess it here. Van Dyck seems to have planned the picture to hang high and be seen from below, which lifts the king above us. The great tree and the horse both seem to bow to him.
At the lower right an inscription names him Charles I, King of Great Britain. It presents a monarch more than a huntsman, an odd fit for a picture billed as "the king at the hunt".

context.text: For a long time no one knew who this was. A 1746 inventory called the picture a portrait of "an armed prince" by Titian. An inventory of 1857 listed the sitter as unknown, and a later catalogue named the wrong count. He is now identified as Juan Francisco Alfonso de Pimentel, Count and Duke of Benavente, one of Spain's senior commanders.

The Titian guess was not far-fetched: the portrait is close in design and technique to Titian's portrait of Philip II of 1551. Whether Velázquez painted it is now in doubt, and it is catalogued as attributed to him. The doubts rest on how it is painted: the armour and the sash are handled in different ways, and the curtain meets the landscape awkwardly.

details.text: Unusually for a nobleman's portrait, he wears pieces of armour from the collection of Philip II.

A gold collar rests on his armour. It is identified as the collar of the Order of the Golden Fleece, granted to him in May 1648 as a reward for serving the crown. That honour dates the portrait to just before Velázquez, if he painted it, left on his second journey to Italy.
Everything around him spells out his rank as a commander: the sword at his hip, the general's sash, and on the table his helmet and baton.

context.text: Nobody knows who this arrogant young man is. He must have been one of Bronzino's literary friends in Florence, and the book in his hand is probably poetry. One recent proposal is Bonaccorso di Pietro Pinadori, born in 1502, whom Vasari lists among Bronzino's sitters with Ugolino Martelli and Lorenzo Lenzi. In 1964 Vincenzo Borghini was proposed in conversation. An older idea, that Bronzino painted himself, has not been taken up by later writers.

Even the painter's name has moved. An engraving published in 1812 named the sitter as a Duke of Urbino and the painter as Sebastiano del Piombo, and Lucien Bonaparte's sale in London in 1816 also gave it to Sebastiano. It is now firmly Bronzino's. Most date it to the 1530s, though proposals run from about 1530 to about 1545. Some have guessed that he started it at one time and only finished it later, perhaps years later.

Bronzino also reworked the picture. The most conspicuous change was to the architecture behind the sitter. Much later the dealer Durand-Ruel bought the panel for 140,000 francs and passed it to the Havemeyers for $40,000; it came to the Met with Mrs Havemeyer's bequest in 1929.

details.text: Look at the furniture. A grotesque mask hangs on the front of the table at the left, stretched as though it were cloth rather than stone. Another grotesque head, ram-horned and thick-lipped, juts from the arm of the chair at the right. These faces, drawn from an ancient Roman kind of fantastic ornament, seem meant to set off the sitter's own refined features. A third, mask-like face is said to lurk almost hidden in the folds of his breeches; in this image it is very hard to make out.

His black satin doublet has slashed sleeves and sits over a white shirt with a ruffled collar. A blue belt crosses the waist, and his left hand rests on his hip, the thumb standing free. Below the belt, the codpiece was once more elaborate. An article of clothing, almost certainly a pair of gloves, was originally tucked into it. No gloves show there now.

context.text: Bonnard painted this whole room from memory. He thought of himself as the last of the Impressionists, yet unlike them he did not paint what was in front of him. He put his own response to the scene ahead of what the eye saw.

The room was at Ma Roulotte, 'My Caravan', the house Bonnard bought in 1912 at Vernonnet, a small Seine town. Cats sit on the chairs, and his wife, Marthe de Méligny, rests her arms on the windowsill.

Bonnard sold the picture to the Paris dealers Bernheim-Jeune on 7 November 1913. It stayed with them until at least 1939, then belonged to Gaston Bernheim de Villers. After passing to the New York dealer Sam Salz, it was sold to Minneapolis in 1954.

details.text: The open door and window join the room to the garden. Bonnard links the shapes by bathing them in related hues, so the inside and the outside seem to flow together.
Look for the cats. Two pale ones sit on the wooden chair at the right, one faint and low on the seat; a third peeps over the edge of the table on the left.
Marthe leans in on the sill from outside, in a red top, between the room and the garden.

context.text: Murillo lived among the friars while he worked. In 1665 the Franciscans of Seville's Capuchin convent hired him to paint the pictures for their church, and he moved in with his assistants. Work stopped, then resumed in 1668 with the paintings for the side altars, finished in 1669. This one was made for the second chapel on the left of the nave.

The series was scattered after the Napoleonic invasion. Most of it reached Seville's fine arts museum when church property was confiscated, a seizure dated to 1835 in one account and recorded as 1840 for this picture. A Seville exhibition later brought the whole series together for the first time since.

details.text: As a reward for Francis giving up worldly goods, Christ pulls his right arm free of the nail and draws the saint to him.
Francis plants his foot on the globe, rejecting earthly things. The angels' book makes the same point: whoever does not give up everything he owns cannot be Christ's disciple.
X-rays reveal how Murillo worked. They show luminous outlines around the main figures, very clear in this picture, and changes of mind about some parts, including Christ's feet.
A restoration removed oxidised varnish that had turned yellow and hidden the original colours. It also showed that the canvas is made of two different linen weaves.

context.text: In 1714 this Susanna was in the collection of the painter Benedetto Luti. He had a copy made and sent it to an adviser of Lothar Franz von Schönborn, asking if the original would make a fit present for the German patron. The answer was yes, and the painting went to Pommersfelden, where it still is.
But it went there credited to Orazio Gentileschi, though it carries his daughter Artemisia's signature. One study ties the gift to Luti's negotiations to be made a knight of the Holy Roman Empire.
This is Artemisia's first painting of the subject, from 1610, and it is still her best-known version of it.

details.text: Susanna is naked and distressed, her raised hands fending the elders off. Her face shows pain, and her refusal to give in to their blackmail.
Above her the two men lean over the wall with their heads together; one raises a finger to his lips.
On the stone at the lower left is a faint painted inscription: the signature that the 1714 gift ignored.

context.text: The bishop who ordered this picture did not care for its sky. The Bishop of Salisbury, Dr John Fisher, asked Constable for it in 1820, and his unease at the dark clouds that animate the sky was what finally forced a reworking.

After it was shown at the Royal Academy in 1823, Constable was asked to paint it again, smaller, and also at full size. A new, sunnier version went to the bishop's daughter as a wedding present; a third was still unfinished when the bishop died in May 1825.

Constable had dreaded the job, calling it 'the most difficult subject in landscape I ever had upon my easil'. The three versions have been read as a sign of a gap opening between his expressive vision and his patron's picturesque taste.

details.text: At the gate on the left stand, it is now thought, the bishop and his wife. Further along the path is a daughter of theirs, most likely Dolly.
In the meadow some of the cattle drink at a pond, under the shelter of tall trees.
Look at the sky: heavy grey cloud, darkest just to the right of the spire. It was clouds like these that troubled the bishop.

context.text: Rubens painted this view of his own estate for his own delight. A diplomat as well as a painter, ennobled in both Spain and England, he had bought the manor of Het Steen, near Mechelen, in 1635. The picture celebrates what mattered most to him: perhaps his own success, but also the peace and prosperity of his native Flanders.

We can be reasonably sure it was never a commission. Its support seems to have been patched together from small, unevenly shaped panels, probably oak, added and pinned as Rubens went along, a method no collector would accept. It was almost certainly painted as the partner of his Landscape with a Rainbow, today in London's Wallace Collection.
The pair are thought to have hung facing each other in one room of Rubens's house, and an exhibition reunited them in 2021. Constable knew this picture and admired it.

details.text: The sun has only just risen. It glints on the manor's windows and on the gun of the man in front, crouching with his dog to shoot the partridges nearby.
A couple head for market on their sturdy cart, the wife perched high on the load.
Further back, the lord and lady of Het Steen are out walking; a nursemaid holds the baby, while in the moat someone fishes for breakfast.

The picture's size makes us look twice. Up close, we share the crouching hunter's view, though his partridges seem closer to us than to him. From afar, the sunrise on the right marks the east, as on a map.

context.text: To paint this, Rosa Bonheur went to the Paris horse market twice a week for a year and a half. She had police permission to wear men's clothes, to avoid drawing attention.

The picture caused a sensation at the Salon of 1853; one critic felt he ought to leap clear of the horses. In London in 1855 another marvelled that 'so masculine a work is the production of a feminine hand', and it was shown privately at Buckingham Palace at Queen Victoria's request.

After some critics found it unfinished, Bonheur retouched the ground, trees and sky in 1855, which is probably why the date reads '1853.5'. In 1887 Cornelius Vanderbilt bought it at auction and gave it to the Met, where it has been a favourite ever since.

details.text: She painted huge working horses, not riding horses, caught as they wheel round to stride back up the boulevard.
Part of the inspiration was the Parthenon: Bonheur said the friezes came to mind in a crowd of dealers trying out their horses.
The market was held on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital, by the Salpêtrière asylum, whose dome rises in the left background.

context.text: Vasnetsov conceived the picture in the summer of 1880, while staying with his brother at Akhtyrka near Moscow. A barefoot peasant girl with big, sad eyes, whom he saw and sketched there, set off the idea. An exhibition catalogue listed it as 'Alyonushka (the little fool)'.

Critics took her as a type of the orphaned village girl; one guessed Vasnetsov meant a girl from Russian fairy tales. In 1882 he reworked it, and an X-ray shows something of the changes: her face, neck and shoulder were repainted, and the landscape was touched in many places.
Tretyakov did not buy it then; A. I. Mamontov did, for 500 roubles. In 1900 the gallery's council paid 8,000 for it.

details.text: No particular story is told; what comes through is the spirit of the Russian fairy tale, set in the quiet landscape of central Russia.
She has sat on the stone so long that she seems to have turned to stone with grief.
Look into the pool: a faint reflection shows in the dark water, which seems to pull her in.

context.text: When this picture was shown, senior members of the Wanderers' circle loudly objected: Nesterov, they said, had brought an icon to an art exhibition, a thing for a church and for believers. They urged Tretyakov not to buy it. He bought it from the artist in 1890 anyway.

The subject is a religious legend: the boy Bartholomew, later Saint Sergius of Radonezh, struggles to learn to read until a mysterious old monk gives him the gift of wisdom. The idea came from the artist E. D. Polenova, who was planning illustrated lives of the saints for ordinary readers.
Nesterov's model for the boy was a girl he came across, almost by chance, in the village of Komyakino. He recalled her as about ten, short-haired and frail, with big blue eyes full of wonder.

details.text: The pale shirt of the slender boy draws the eye first; the dark monk beside the oak seems almost part of the tree.
His face is lost in the shadow of his hood; we see a halo and a glimpse of white beard, and the miracle stays mysterious.
While working, Nesterov stayed near the Trinity monastery linked with Saint Sergius. The muted colours can feel like early spring or late autumn.

context.text: This picture by the young Serov caused a stir among artists and has been seen as an early sign of Impressionism in Russia. It won first prize in a Moscow competition in 1888.

The sitter is Vera, the young daughter of the railway magnate and patron Savva Mamontov. Serov had spent long stretches at the Mamontovs' estate at Abramtsevo since 1885 and was treated as one of the family; he started her portrait in mid-August 1887 and worked on it for more than a month.
He wanted, he said, “that special freshness which you always feel in nature and do not see in pictures”.

details.text: The peaches came from the Abramtsevo greenhouse. With the fallen maple leaves beside them, they mark the end of summer.
Behind her, at the left of the picture, stands a little painted wooden nutcracker soldier, bought at a fair and painted by Serov himself, a nod to Hoffmann's tale.
Her face is finely finished, while the background, her fingers and the fruit are painted fast and loose; the light from the window seems to fill the room.

context.text: After a hunt, Diana has made her nymph Callisto undress to bathe, and finds she is pregnant. On the goddess's orders the others hold Callisto down and pull her clothes away, baring her swollen belly.

Titian made it, with its partner Diana and Actaeon, for Philip II of Spain, the most powerful of his patrons, in 1556–59. The pair seem to have been meant to hang together: the landscape and the stream carry on from one to the other.

In 1623 the two were crated up as diplomatic presents for Prince Charles, the future Charles I, then in Madrid courting the Spanish Infanta. In 1704 Philip V presented them to France's ambassador, and they went on to the Duc d'Orléans. The two British national galleries bought them jointly in 2009 and 2012.

details.text: Diana's right arm shoots out, one finger pointing at Callisto.
Titian kept reworking the group around Callisto as he painted, shifting poses and adding or taking away clothes until it looked right.
Damage has blurred Diana and Callisto themselves more than anyone else; both have lost some of their solidity through paint loss.

context.text: Bougival, a village on the Seine west of Paris, had open-air cafés popular with city people. Its reputation was somewhat dubious.
Renoir painted three large dance pictures, and this is probably the last to be finished and the most romantic. Suzanne Valadon posed for the woman; one account names Renoir's brother as her partner.
As soon as it was ready, it was sent to an exhibition in London, at Dowdeswell's gallery in 1883. The Boston museum bought it in 1937 for $150,000.

details.text: Look at their hands: no gloves. That bare touch, and how close their faces are, would have looked daring to people at the time.
His straw hat hides his eyes, so his body does the talking. Renoir, the son of a tailor and a dressmaker, takes care over her clothes, down to the purple fruits on her red bonnet.
The dance floor is a mess: cigarette ends, spent matches, and a little posy of flowers dropped on the ground.

context.text: Brown got the idea from watching navvies dig drains in Hampstead. The result is a picture of work in all its forms, and of those who do none.
This is a smaller version. The patron James Leathart ordered it in 1859 for £315, and Brown signed and dated it 1863; the larger original is in Manchester.

The two are close, but Brown made one notable change. In the original, his wife Emma posed for the lady with the blue parasol; here he put in Maria Leathart, his patron's wife. When Leathart lent the picture to a Newcastle institute in 1866, a local paper dismissed it as “one of the extraordinary mistakes of the present day”.

details.text: At the right stand the 'brainworkers', the preacher F. D. Maurice and the writer Thomas Carlyle. They look idle, but Brown saw them as the source of reform.
Not everyone here is working. Under the trees at right, men with no work lie asleep on the bank, while a rich man and his daughter ride by at the back.
The potboy carrying beer has a copy of The Times tucked under his arm.

context.text: “This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise, with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big,” Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo. The window was in the asylum at Saint-Rémy, where he stayed for a year, 1889–90, hoping for relief from his mental illness.

The picture both records what he saw and breaks away from it. He painted it in mid-June over several sessions by day, not at night. The village was not visible from his window; he based it on other views, and the cypress stands much closer than it really was.

details.text: The sky fills three-quarters of the canvas, rolling like waves. The bright moon is at the right and Venus, the morning star, at centre left.
Look at the church steeple, tall and sharp. It looks like a Dutch spire from his homeland, not a French one.
The flame-shaped cypress shoots up almost to the top edge, tying earth to sky. Some read it as a bridge between life below and death, or heaven, above.

context.text: Wood posed his sister and his dentist as a farmer and his daughter, stiff and old-fashioned, like “tintypes from my old family album.” Behind them is a house in the 1880s style called Carpenter Gothic; he had seen one like it in Eldon, Iowa.
Its debut at the Art Institute in 1930 made Wood famous overnight and earned him a $300 prize. He came to be counted a leader of Regionalism, painting rural American life.

What did it mean? Many viewers took it as satire, mocking Midwesterners left behind by the modern world. Wood meant the opposite: a positive picture of rural values, and reassurance at the start of the Great Depression.

details.text: Their eyes go different ways. One reading has him gripping the pitchfork like a weapon and challenging us, while she holds rigid and looks away.
Look at the bottom right, on his overalls: Wood signed and dated the picture there, in light blue paint.

context.text: Five years after his first portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer, Klimt painted her again. Now she stands squarely, strong and self-assured. It was his first major commissioned portrait in the modern style of his last years.

In 2006, after an arbitration ruling, it was among five paintings returned to the Bloch-Bauer heirs. It was auctioned that year for $87.9 million, and in 2016 it sold privately for $150 million. It has stayed in private collections ever since; in 2023 it was cleaned at the Belvedere, which removed a grey film and revived its pinks, greens and blues.

details.text: Klimt struggled with it. X-rays and infrared show a first version in which she stood on an oval carpet, closer to us, in a much fuller dress, with a feathered hat spreading out to the edge of the canvas.
Behind her, Klimt fills the wall with floral colour and Asian ornament: little horsemen and a pavilion on red, above a green field of flowers.

context.text: She laughs with her mouth open and her teeth on show. In Calvinist Holland, under the manners of the day, no portrait could show a sitter like that. Hals, known as the master of laughter, painted grins like this mostly on folksy characters. One reading hears her laugh as drunk and unbridled, a breach of the morals of her time that could only be painted in someone on the margins.

She was real. An inscription on the back, probably from the 17th century, calls her Malle Babbe of Haarlem, and recent archive research identified her as Barbara Claes, who died in 1663. Malle means mad. She was a notorious figure in town, and Hals probably knew her. The picture is a likeness of one real woman and, at the same time, a picture of a kind of person. It is now dated 1640–1646; an earlier dating put it at 1633/35.

In 1646 she was sent, for immoral behaviour, to the Haarlem werkhuis, a madhouse, poorhouse and prison in one, on the edge of town. She spent 15 years there altogether. Some years after this picture was painted, one of Hals's sons and his eldest daughter were admitted to the same place.

details.text: Look at the owl on her shoulder. It probably stands for drunkenness: the Dutch said someone was “zoo beschonken als een uil”, as drunk as an owl.

Compare her face with her collar and sleeves. The face is worked up in denser paint, but the collar is a scribble of separate white strokes and the sleeves are only roughed in. That loose, abrupt handling helps it feel like a moment caught by chance.

context.text: She was sixteen or seventeen, and the mistress of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, who commissioned the portrait. Cecilia Gallerani was a lady-in-waiting. Her affair with the duke ran from 1489 to 1491, but the duke was betrothed to Princess Beatrice d'Este, and he married her in January 1491. That year Cecilia had his son, Cesare, and mother and child were sent away from court.

Portraits until then mostly showed sitters in profile. Leonardo turned her three-quarters and let her glance at someone we cannot see, so she seems caught in a slight movement. That gave her a life not seen in portraits before. It is among just over a dozen portraits by him that survive.

Adam Jerzy Czartoryski bought it in Italy around 1800, and from 1809 it hung in the Gothic House at Puławy. In September 1939 the Nazis looted it, meaning it for Hitler's planned museum in Linz. The governor-general Hans Frank kept it through the war, probably at Wawel, his residence. A military mission tracked it down in Bavaria after the war, and it came home to Kraków in 1946, without the Raphael taken along with it, which had gone missing.

details.text: The ermine may be a coded message. In 1488 Ludovico had been given the Order of the Ermine by the King of Naples, and one of his nicknames was Ermellino Bianco, the white ermine. So the animal in her arms may stand for the duke himself, and for their intimacy. Ermines also meant purity, and gale, the Greek word for the animal, sounds like the start of her surname.

The black background is not Leonardo's. It was painted over in the 19th century, when the dark trim on her dress and ribbons was also reinforced. Studies so far find a plain blue-grey under the black, with no view behind her, darkening from right to left. Lit that way, she once came softly out of half-darkness instead of being cut out against black.

Look at the yellow capitals at the top left: LA BELE FERONIERE over LEONARD D'AWINCI. Leonardo was known as the painter from the start, but who the sitter was stayed uncertain until the end of the 19th century. Archive research settled it, drawing among other things on a sonnet by Bernardo Bellincioni and on letters from her to Isabella d'Este.

context.text: The king asked for Horace victorious. David went to Rome and came back with an oath instead: three brothers pledging before their father to serve the State and, if need be, to die for it. The format changed too, from the square canvas first ordered to a far wider one, more than four metres across.

The signature gives the year 1784, yet the work was probably painted in the first half of 1785 and only finished that July. Romans saw it first, in David's own studio. Then it was shipped to the Paris Salon of 1785, where the booklet noted it was for the King. No other picture did as much to put him at the top of his profession.

When the Salon closed, David took it back to paint his own replica, now in Toledo. Ordered for the king, the original stayed in the painter's hands: it hung in his Louvre studio until 1791, and only in December 1797 did the Muséum central des arts claim it from him, along with his Brutus.

details.text: Start at bottom left, on a floor slab: David signed in Latin, naming Rome and the year MDCCLXXXIV, 1784. In this image the second line reads Roma, where the Louvre transcribes Romae. Even signing in Latin was a Neoclassical touch.
Follow the arms. Their hands and the father's gleaming swords meet at the centre, set off by bright light, while he turns his eyes upward, to the gods.

Now compare the two halves. The men are built from hard, straight lines. The women and children on the right are all soft curves, slumped against one another, and it is they who carry the feeling and the doubt.

context.text: The sultan wanted surrender and got mockery instead. As the story goes, in 1675 the Turkish sultan sent a threatening letter to the Zaporozhian Cossacks, ordering them to give themselves up 'voluntarily and without any resistance.' They answered with a reply full of jokes and contempt, promising 'to fight on land and water.'

Repin first heard the tale in 1878 and made a sketch that same year. The picture then took him more than a decade, thirteen years by one count. He went to Ukraine, dug through archives and history books, and gathered folk tales about how the Cossack host lived. While he painted, his favourite masters, Velázquez and Hals, were on his mind.

A picture of defiance ended up in the hands of an emperor. Alexander III bought the finished canvas, and it was kept in the Winter Palace. In 1895 it won gold medals in Munich and Budapest, and in 1897 Nicholas II gave it to the Russian Museum.

details.text: Look at the table. The man bent over the paper with a quill is the scribe, and the face Repin gave him began as a study of a real person: the historian D. I. Yavornytsky.

Other laughers also began as studies of real people, whom Repin then transformed completely. The big man in the red coat and white fur hat, holding his stomach, started from A. I. Rubets, a professor at the conservatory. At left, the moustached Cossack with his fist on a comrade's bare back was first the painter Ya. F. Tsionglinsky.

context.text: The ship stuck in the ice is a real one: the SS United States, which belonged to the polar explorer Isaac Israel Hayes. Hayes was Church's friend, and in 1861, home again from the far north, he gave the painter his own sketches as inspiration. Church had also watched the northern lights for himself, sketching them on Mount Desert Island in Maine in 1860.

He finished it in 1865, around the time the Civil War ended that April. Northern lights rarely show far to the south. When they did during the war, many people read them as a sign that God stood against the slaveholding Confederacy, a sign of how much rode on the Union winning. Several readings tie the painting to the war.

That spring also brought private grief. Church and his wife lost both their children to diphtheria: Herbert, aged two, and Emma, five months old. The same year he painted Sunrise and Moonrise in their honour. Whether this sky is a third picture of mourning is an open question.

details.text: Find the dog sled: a few dark specks on the ice just right of the ship. It holds out a hope that help could reach the frozen ship.
Look closely at the ship. One small orange light glows on board: a sign of life inside what the sled hints may be a prison of ice.

context.text: The goddess of love is fast asleep, out in the open country. Girolamo Marcello probably ordered the picture from Giorgione when he married Morosina Pisani in 1507. Latin wedding verse may explain why she sleeps: such poems call on the slumbering Venus to get up, come to the celebrations and help the newlyweds' love along.

Giorgione died before he could complete it. A document of 1525 records that he started the canvas and that Titian, who worked with him, brought it to an end. So the picture credited with founding the tradition of reclining female nudes came from two hands. When it was first entered in an inventory, in 1722–28, it was listed simply as a Titian. Nobody can now say exactly where one painter stops and the other begins: the picture has been restored so often that its condition no longer allows a reliable answer.

Its travels were not over. In the Second World War it was stored first at the Albrechtsburg in Meissen, then from 1943 in an unused railway tunnel. In July 1945 Soviet trophy teams took it to the USSR. It spent the next ten years in Moscow and came back to Dresden in 1956.

details.text: Trace her outline from the raised elbow down to her feet. The same soft, rolling line carries on through the hills behind her, and figure and land settle into one idyllic calm.
Look at what she lies on: a deep red cushion and a crumpled white sheet. They may be Titian's work, along with the landscape, though after so many restorations no one can be sure.

Now look at the grass beyond her feet. A Cupid once sat there, playing with his bow and arrow. By 1837 the figure was so badly damaged that it was covered over with meadow green, and only X-rays still pick up fragments of him.

context.text: There is nothing here but a dog, and only its head at that. No human figure explains the scene. Its museum title is The Drowning Dog, but it is also known simply as A Dog. The rest of the body may be struggling below, in something that might be earth, sand or water.

Goya painted it straight onto a wall of the Quinta del Sordo, the country estate near Madrid he had bought in 1819, as one of the series now called the Black Paintings. It sat on the upper floor beside a door, on its right according to one catalogue. Chemical analysis has found oil in these murals, so the technique was apparently mixed.
Later the murals were taken off the walls and moved onto canvas. The transfer did them great harm, and a large amount of paint was lost.

details.text: Look how small the head is against the empty space above it. The scene has been linked to the idea that death cannot be escaped.

Now follow the dog's eyes. Its muzzle tilts up to the right, at something we cannot see. According to one catalogue, a photographic negative of the mural shows what it was: two birds in flight, which vanished when the painting was moved to canvas. The empty space may be partly the work of damage, not of Goya.

context.text: Gauguin did not invent this Christ. He took the figure from a seventeenth-century carved and painted crucifix in the old Trémalo Chapel, close to Pont-Aven in Brittany. He made its yellow stronger and moved it out of doors, into a vivid autumn countryside. Brittany was his first move away from Paris, and what he painted there broke sharply with Impressionism.
The season matters. In Brittany the harvest carried spiritual weight: people believed grain went through the same stages as a Christian life, from birth and life to death and rebirth.

By the time of an auction on 22 February 1891, Emile Schuffenecker had already bought the picture, so it was not in the sale. In 1940 the German army confiscated it from Paul Rosenberg, and in June 1944 it was sent from Paris to Baden-Baden for Goering. It went back to Rosenberg after the war, and in 1946 the Albright Art Gallery in Buffalo bought it from him.

details.text: The cross does not stand in the middle. Its post rises left of centre, and its crossbar runs off the left edge of the canvas. For a Crucifixion, that is an unusual placement.
