Look at the women around its foot, in white caps and the dress of their region. The two at left sit with their hands folded; the third turns her back to us. The museum places the scene at the evening hour of the Angelus, a daily Catholic prayer.
And why yellow? Set against the dark brown wood, the body glows a sickly-sweet yellow. Gauguin said the colour carried what he felt about the peasants' piety and their isolated lives.

context.text: All that effort, and one fox. It dangles from a spear over a hunter's shoulder as the men and their worn-out dogs head down toward the village in the valley.
Bruegel put his name and the date, 1565, at the bottom centre. The first owner on record is Nicolaas Jongelinck. In 1594 the city of Antwerp made the picture a gift to Archduke Ernst.

It is counted as the first winter landscape in European painting, and the most prominent one. The country is northern, but it is not Bruegel's flat Netherlands. It is an ideal world, and we look out across its vast distances from high above.

details.text: Look left, outside the house with the hanging sign. People are feeding straw to a blazing fire. According to the museum it is meant for singeing a pig, though the pig itself is nowhere to be seen.
Then drop down into the valley. On the frozen ponds, dozens of tiny figures skate and play. Details like these have done much to make the picture so popular.
Look up at the black birds in the bare branches, and the one gliding out over the valley. Sky and ice share the same grey-green, and the whole scene gives the impression of a cold that never ends.

context.text: The cathedral is not finished. Its front catches the sun while a storm darkens the sky behind, and one of its two towers still stops short. The design echoes Strasbourg and Reims, and most of all Cologne, whose cathedral then stood incomplete.

Schinkel painted it in 1815 and linked the church, with its one unfinished tower, to a ruler's festive entry into his residence. Most likely the scene stands for Prussia's King Friedrich Wilhelm III, returning victorious from the wars against Napoleon.
One reading takes the storm as God's verdict on Napoleon. In the same reading the unfinished cathedral is the state, a building that still has to be completed.

details.text: Look at the crowd in the lower left: armoured riders, white horses, a gilded carriage and a blue canopy topped with white plumes, all pressing up the slope toward a bridge. This is the prince and his retinue, said to be entering the castle at the left edge, and probably a stand-in for the king's return.
Now look at the top of the left-hand tower. Where its spire should be, there is scaffolding, and from it flies a white flag. The flag carries the imperial eagle, too small to make out here.
Follow the rainbow. It rises near the castle on the left and arches high over the cathedral, heading for the medieval city on the right, though it leaves the canvas before it gets there.

context.text: Two women sit talking at a table by the window on a lunch break, while another couple is half hidden at the back. Hopper pares an everyday midday eating place down to a couple of tables and the people at them. Chinese restaurants he had been to were likely the spark.
Like several of his best-known pictures from the years around 1929, it has no known drawings. Its roots lie in how French Impressionist and Ashcan painters showed city life.

Barney A. Ebsworth bought it in 1973, and Seattle's art museum hoped to receive it among the gifts he had promised. That did not happen. After his death it sold at Christie's New York on 13 November 2018 for $91.88 million, a record for Hopper, to another private owner.

details.text: Look out of the window. It is the sign, not the food, that sets the scene: only part of it shows, but its bold SUEY names the kind of place this is.

Now find the third woman, easy to miss: only her face and red hat show at the far left edge, across the back table from the man in the dark suit. All three women were posed by the same model, Hopper's wife, Jo.

context.text: As a young man at the peak of his fame, Rembrandt painted himself as a reveller, goblet raised and his beloved on his lap. Here he takes up the parable of the son who comes home wretched and worn out, and kneels before a father who bends over him in forgiveness. One reading sees this canvas as the final chapter of that earlier story.

Nobody commissioned it. Holland was Protestant, its churches had no painted altarpieces, and large religious pictures were rarely made, yet he produced a canvas more than two and a half metres tall. It entered the Hermitage in 1766, from the collection of Catherine the Great.

It is dated around 1668, just months before his death, though it has also been placed about 1662 and about 1669. Some believe it was among his very last paintings and was left unfinished. It has even been catalogued as the work of Rembrandt and a follower. After his death, someone tried to finish a Prodigal Son of his. It may have been this one.

details.text: Look at the son. Like a penitent, he has had his head shaved; his once-fine clothes hang in tatters, and his face is pressed into his father's chest, turned away from us. One foot is bare, its sole toward the viewer, and the shoe lies beside it.

In the gloom the father's face glows, and the light on the son's back reads as comfort. His red cloak spreads over the kneeling figure like a canopy, and both his hands rest on his son's shoulders. Around them, the onlookers watch without a word.

context.text: Are these lovers on their way to the island of love, or on their way home? On the older reading, the one the familiar title follows, the couples are setting out for Cythera, somewhere in the mist. A more recent reading turns the scene round: they are already on the island and getting ready to go back to ordinary life, which brings out the picture's melancholy. Even the name is double. At the Louvre its main title is Pèlerinage à l'île de Cythère, a pilgrimage to the island; L'embarquement pour Cythère, the Embarkation, comes second.

Watteau kept the Académie Royale waiting for it. His talent won him membership in 1712, but the reception piece he owed arrived in 1717, five years on, and only after he had been asked again and again.

Once handed in, it stayed with the Academy. Through the rest of the eighteenth century it hung at the Louvre in the room where the Academy met, until the Academy's collections were seized in 1795 and it went with them.

details.text: Find the woman in the golden dress near the middle, standing beside a man in pink. She glances back over her shoulder, toward the couples behind her.

context.text: Nobody knows whose funeral this is. Courbet painted a village burial as if it were a scene from history. The canvas is 315 by 668 centimetres, and the villagers are life-size. Painters usually kept that scale for people from the Bible or from myth. Nor did he flatter anyone.

He started in autumn 1849 in a studio at Ornans that his father had fitted out, and he grumbled about the poor light and the lack of room to step back. Local people, he said, all wanted to pose, and about fifty of them fill the picture. Behind them is the landscape that can still be seen from the Ornans cemetery.

At the Salon of 1850–51 some critics called it naive or brutal and compared it to the huge painted canvases on fairground booths. It stands as a manifesto of a new way of painting, Realism. Even its subject stays open: one suggestion is that it may stand for the Bonapartists burying the Second Republic.

details.text: Look closely at the cloth, the soil and the cliffs. Courbet built their textures out of thick paint, laid on with a brush or a palette knife.
Now find the two men in red robes and tall red hats just right of the priest. They are beadles. Their faces are as flushed as their robes, and the critics laughed at them.
A skull lies on the turned earth at the bottom edge, beside the mourners' feet.

context.text: Sargent was supposed to paint 'Anglo-American co-operation'. The British government had asked him for the central picture in a planned Hall of Remembrance for the First World War. He could find nothing suitable for that theme, so he painted something he had seen with his own eyes: men after a mustard gas attack, in August 1918, on the Western Front.

He had crossed to France that July with a fellow artist, Henry Tonks. Back in his London studio, he finished the canvas by March 1919. It is enormous: about 2.3 metres high and more than six metres wide, the largest painting the Imperial War Museums hold.

When it went on public view in May 1919, its realism is said to have left some people feeling physically sick. Over 2022 and 2023, conservators cleaned it bit by bit, going over each small patch six to eight times to lift off dirt and varnish. Underneath were pinks and blues: the light of a clear evening as the sun goes down.

details.text: Look between the legs of the blinded men, far off. A football match is going on in the evening sun. Since the cleaning, the players can be seen as two teams in different shirts.
Look at the faces of the men in the line, half hidden by bandages, and at the wounded men lying all round them. One reading finds a hint of rescue in the scene, but sees loss and suffering above all.
Now look at the bottom left corner. The signature reads 'John S. Sargent Aug 1918', the month of the attack, though the painting was not finished until the following spring.

context.text: Waterhouse gave each siren a woman's head on a bird's body. The idea came from an ancient Greek vase, now in the British Museum in London. One critic pointed out that Homer has two sirens; the painting has seven.
To hear their song and survive, Ulysses had himself tied to the mast, and his men stopped up their ears so the ship could get past.

In June 1891 Sir Hubert Herkomer bought it for Melbourne's National Gallery of Victoria for £1200, straight from that year's Royal Academy show. Once it reached Melbourne, local critics attacked the liberties Waterhouse had taken with the Greek legend, and held up the purchase as proof that the gallery's trustees were misusing public money.

details.text: Look at the oarsmen. Most have a cloth bound around their heads, and one siren has landed on the side of the ship to lean in close to a rower's face.
Look at the far lower right, just right of the painted eye on the hull: Waterhouse signed and dated the canvas there in black paint. It still sits in the frame it had when it left the Royal Academy.

context.text: A year after he signed this canvas, Sánchez Cotán walked away from a successful workshop in Toledo and entered the Carthusian order as a lay brother. He dated it 1602, while he was at the height of his powers. For a still life, 1602 is a very early date.

The setting is a hollow of stone, probably a cupboard where fresh food was stored. Behind everything is pure black. A light from one side picks out each lemon, root and feather and throws hard shadows, a dramatic contrast of dark and light that looks ahead to Caravaggio.

The picture later belonged to the Infante Sebastián Gabriel and passed down through his family. In 1991 the Prado acquired it from the heirs of the Duke of Hernani, using money from the Villaescusa Legacy. Back in 1603, the painter drew up a list of what he owned. One entry is a canvas ‘of the thistle where the partridges are’, named there as the model for other versions. Thistle and partridges fill this canvas too, but the list does not say which version it was.

details.text: Look at the front face of the ledge, between the hanging radish roots and the base of the thistle. The painter’s name and the year 1602 are lettered there on the stone.
Look at the front edge of the ledge. A carrot, the radishes and the thistle all stick out past it, into our space. The aim was a perfect illusion.

context.text: These two panels were not made to hang side by side on their own. Technical study shows they began as the side wings of a triptych, or as the doors of a tabernacle or a shrine for relics.

The patrons were most likely Philip the Good, duke of Burgundy, and Isabella of Portugal. Jan van Eyck was Philip’s court painter. Who painted them is not entirely settled: they are most often given to Van Eyck, or to Van Eyck helped by his workshop. The Met now dates them about 1436–38. Earlier, they were credited to Van Eyck and an unnamed assistant and dated a few years later, about 1440–41.

Their travels were long. They were very probably the pair acquired during a viceroy’s term in Naples between 1637 and 1641 and carried to Madrid in 1643. Later the Russian ambassador to Spain, Dmitry Tatishchev, bought them as Van Eyck’s work from a convent near Madrid, or possibly near Burgos, and left them to the Imperial Hermitage. In 1933 the Hermitage sold them, through a New York dealer, to the Met. Along the way the paint itself moved: in 1867, at the Hermitage, it was taken off its wooden panels and put onto canvas.

details.text: In the left panel, look at the small white board on the cross above Christ’s head. Its three lines are in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and the Latin is cut short: IHC NAZAR… REX IVDE…

In the right panel, look at the red robe below Christ’s raised hands. Gold letters run down it twice, once on each side, in Latin. They are a line from Matthew’s Gospel: “Come, ye blessed of my Father.”

context.text: “Swim in the white free abyss, infinity is before you.” Malevich wrote those words in a manifesto that came out alongside the first public showing of this series, in Moscow in 1919. He was elated.

He called his theory Suprematism, “the supremacy of pure feeling or perception in the pictorial arts.” He coined the word in 1915 for a new abstract painting that dropped every reference to the world outside. This canvas was among the first to propose that a modern picture need not refer to anything outside itself, and that geometric shapes, carefully placed, could suggest motion and boundless space.

Aircraft fascinated him, and he studied photographs taken from the air. He wanted this picture to give a sense of floating and of rising above the everyday; white, he believed, was the colour of infinity. MoMA acquired it in 1935, and the acquisition was confirmed in 1999 by an agreement with Malevich’s estate.

details.text: Look closely and the edges of the square are slightly soft and uneven, not crisply ruled. Without a hard border, the white around it seems to go on without end. Set askew and off-centre, the square looks as if it is drifting.
Now look at the paint itself. Both whites are laid on in visible brushstrokes, with small ridges and an uneven surface. For all its austerity, the picture keeps the trace of the painter’s hand.

context.text: The tombs are real. They belong to Beth Haim, the burial ground of Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish community at Ouderkerk aan de Amstel, sited there since 1616, and they survive there now. Almost everything else Ruisdael made up: the rolling hills, the mountain stream, the ruins.

Why invent a setting? It turns a graveyard into an allegory. Neglected tombs, a ruined church, storm clouds and a rainbow all point to the same idea, that nothing on earth lasts. Painters often made that point, called vanitas, in still lifes, with a skull, a book, a flower or a candle. Carrying it in a landscape is unusual.

Nearly two metres wide, it is one of Ruisdael's best-known pictures. The museum dates it to 1654 or 1655, though one account places it about 1660 to 1670. Julius H. Haass gave it to Detroit in his brother's memory.

details.text: Look for the large white tomb at the centre, catching the sunlight. It marks the grave of a doctor, Eliahu Montalto, who died in 1616, the same year the cemetery was founded.
The tall church ruin standing out against the clouds anchors the whole composition. No such building ever stood at the cemetery.
Ruisdael signed the picture on a tomb. Look at the dark tomb at lower left: his name is written in script on the rounded end of its lid.

context.text: “I am nauseated by old walls and old palaces,” Boccioni wrote in 1907. “I want the new, the expressive, the formidable.” Formidable is the right word for this canvas, about three metres wide. It can be read as a hymn of joy to industry and heavy building work. It was painted in 1910, though it is sometimes placed in 1910–11.
In March 1912 a Berlin couple, the Busonis, bought it at the Sackville Gallery in London. Their son Rafaello, in New York, later had it, and he sold it to the Museum of Modern Art in 1951.

Boccioni, one of the most gifted of the young Futurists, did not live long after it. He and Marinetti had hailed the war as healthy for civilisation. In 1916, in the middle of it, he fell off his horse during a cavalry exercise in Verona and died.

details.text: The red horse is the engine of the picture. It is all muscle, yet it seems to come apart under its own force, dissolving into flickering strokes of paint.
Look at the men around the horses. They twist and lean back with their whole weight, pulling on taut ropes against the animals' force.

context.text: Nobody can be sure what Vermeer wanted this picture to say. It begins as a studio scene, a man painting a young woman, and turns into an allegory of painting itself. She poses as Clio, Muse of history, with the trumpet and the book that mark the figure of History. The painter has his back to us. It is tempting to say he is Vermeer, but nothing indicates it. His clothes are elegant and expensive.

In one reading, Clio is the painter’s inspiration. She proclaims how glorious painting had been in the old Netherlands, a glory she has set down in her book of history. The wall map then stands for a land whose fame always rested on its painters. Some have also taken the Muse of history as proof that Vermeer, whatever his own kind of art, still bowed to the art that tradition ranked noblest. Others are not persuaded.

Its title is old. It was already called The Art of Painting in 1676, when his widow, Catharina Bolnes, handed it to her mother, Maria Thins, soon after his death, trying to keep it from creditors. In 1940 Adolf Hitler bought it from Count Jaromir Czernin for a museum he planned at Linz, which was never built. In 1946 it was handed over to the Kunsthistorisches Museum. In 2011, after the Czernin family sought its return, Austria’s culture ministry decided the restitution law did not apply to it.

details.text: Look at the easel. His body hides most of the canvas, but you can see what he has begun: Clio’s crown of laurel, painted in blue like the leaves she wears.

The map is a real one, made by Claes Jansz Visscher in 1636. It shows the Seventeen Provinces, a union that had ended back in 1581, when seven provinces in the north broke away from Spanish rule. On its lower strip, just right of her blue robe, is the signature I Ver-Meer, his most elaborate form, used elsewhere only on The Geographer.

The patterned cloth at left is a rug, pulled aside like a curtain so we can see in. Now find the dark knob on the end of the map’s rod, beside her hand. The vanishing point falls between knob and hand, and there Vermeer pushed a pin into the canvas, leaving a tiny hole in the ground layer.

context.text: In 1874 Morisot became the first woman to show work with the Impressionists, and this was one of her pictures in their first exhibition. Hardly anyone noticed it, although some important critics remarked on its grace and elegance. She tried to sell it, without success, and then took it off display.

She painted it in Paris, and her sitters were family: her sister Edma, keeping watch over Edma's sleeping daughter, Blanche. It was the first time a mother and child appeared in Morisot's work. Motherhood went on to become a subject she returned to again and again.

details.text: Look at Edma's hand on the rim of the cradle. She is drawing the fine net across, so that it hangs between us and the baby. We are kept just outside the moment.

Now trace a line downward from her face. Her gaze, her bent arm, mirrored by the baby's arm raised beside its head, and the baby's shut eyes all fall along one diagonal, and the sweep of the curtain in the background repeats it.
The picture never sold, so it stayed in the family. Its last private owner was the sleeping baby herself, Blanche, by then Madame Forget. The Louvre bought it from her in 1930.

context.text: Nothing happens here except light. Falling from the left, it pulls four pots out of the dark and makes them look solid enough to pick up. Apart from that light and the shadows it casts on the ledge, nothing in the picture hints at time.
Zurbarán often let perspective and geometry slip, and here too the space does not quite hold together. Yet few Spanish still lifes of the Golden Age are more often treated as the model of the genre.

There is a twin. The collector Francisco Cambó owned two nearly identical versions; in 1940 this one came to the Prado from him, and the other is in Barcelona, at the Museu d'Art de Catalunya. The Barcelona canvas has survived in slightly better shape, yet the Metropolitan Museum ranks this one as the finer painting.

details.text: Look at the company the cup keeps. It is probably gilded silver, a luxury piece. Beside it stand white earthenware jugs; the first is a water jug of porous clay, which kept its contents cool as moisture seeped through and evaporated. The reddish vase between them came from across the ocean, probably from New Spain, then a Spanish colony in the Americas.

context.text: Nobody can say for sure who the boy is. Jonathan Buttall, the picture's first owner, was once believed to have posed for it, but that has never been confirmed.

A story is told about the colour. Joshua Reynolds told his students at the Royal Academy that blue was a background colour, fit for faraway hills, never for the front of a picture. His rival Gainsborough is said to have answered with this canvas, putting a blue costume in the middle of the foreground, where it glows against warm browns. That, at least, is how the story goes.

In 1921 Henry E. Huntington bought it, paying more than anyone had paid for a painting until then. Its first success came long before. At the Royal Academy in 1770 the costume set London viewers comparing Gainsborough with Van Dyck, and that helped make his name.

details.text: Look at the clothes: slashed sleeves showing white, a lace collar, knee breeches. This was Van Dyck dress, and the picture was Gainsborough's first full-length figure in it. Van Dyck's dazzling portraits of the nobility had changed British painting long before. Gainsborough knew them well; around Bath he could study them in country houses.

Look at the lower right. Study of the canvas in 2018–19, including a digital X-ray, showed that a dog once stood in the design there before it was painted over, leaving the eye on the boy. The X-ray also shows a man's head at top centre, left from an abandoned portrait: Gainsborough reused the canvas. Those changes hint that the picture was his own idea, and that he went on revising it.

Look at the light sliding along the blue satin. It is not one blue but several: ultramarine, smalt and Prussian blue, with perhaps some azurite. Gainsborough laid them in layer over layer, mixing vigorous slashes with fine touches. Cleaning in the same campaign took off overpaint and cloudy varnish, so the brushwork shows clearly again.

context.text: The earliest record of this picture names its figures but tells no story. In 1530 Marcantonio Michiel saw it in the study of the Venetian collector Gabriele Vendramin. He noted it briefly as a little landscape on canvas "con la tempesta con la cingana et il soldato", with the storm, a gypsy woman and a soldier, by "Zorzi de Castelfranco", Giorgione. The painting's title comes from that note. Even the soldier is uncertain: a Vendramin family inventory of 1569 called him a shepherd.

Its date is unsettled as well. Giorgione died in 1510, and the picture has been placed at almost every point of his short career; around 1505–6 is perhaps the likeliest. It stayed in the Vendramin family into the 1600s and only reached the Accademia in 1932. It counts as a sort of archetype for pastoral painting, a new kind of picture that would go on to do very well in Venice.

It has been read as a myth, a Bible episode, an allegory, a literary scene and a political story. So far, none of these readings has won over more than a few specialists. One reading sees a tribute to the Vendramin family, if Gabriele ordered the picture. The woman would be Lavinia with her baby son Silvius, and the man Silvius grown up, leaning on a spear with no point, the mark of a victorious soldier in imperial Rome. Another makes the pair the hunter Iasion and the goddess Ceres, nursing their child, while Jupiter, in anger, appears as the thunderbolt. A third, more tentative, sees a hero's mother cast out of the city with her child and found in the wild by a kindly young shepherd.

details.text: Look past the wooden bridge to the town under the storm. Its pale walls stand out in the flicker of the lightning. Small, faint coats of arms are painted on its towers: look above the gate of the square tower beside the bridge, and on the round tower at the right. They are the arms of the Carrara family, lords of Padua, and of Venice.

Now look at the young man with the staff. He may not have been part of the first plan. X-rays show that Giorgione changed the figures radically as he worked. According to one account of the X-ray, he first painted a naked woman bathing in the very spot where the man now stands. To some, the changes suggest a painter following his imagination rather than illustrating a set subject.

context.text: The young man holds out a picture from an earlier century. The gold-ground saint in his hands is plainly not by Botticelli: it is a fragment of a fourteenth-century altarpiece, and scholars agree that its figure style and tooled punchmarks point to the Sienese painter Bartolomeo Bulgarini. The disc, 10.6 centimetres across, sits in a hollow cut into the panel. Who set it there is disputed. One view holds that Botticelli set it in himself, so that the living youth and the hoary old saint play off each other. Another calls it a modern addition, filling the place of a damaged stucco relief. Damage and restoration at its edges leave the technical evidence unclear, and a third view holds only that it could be original.

It was most probably acquired in Tuscany by Sir Thomas Wynn, later Lord Newborough, but the firm trail starts only in Wales around 1850. It made £810,000 at Christie's in 1982. The Getty had hoped to buy it but, by its chief curator's account, stepped aside after an expert gave the picture to Botticelli's follower Francesco Botticini, a view he apparently later dropped. A study of 1987 has been credited with putting Botticelli's authorship beyond reasonable doubt. In January 2021 the estate of the property billionaire Sheldon Solow sent it to Sotheby's in New York. The $92.2 million price set a Botticelli auction record, and the buyer was not named.

Nor is it certain who the young man is. In 1950 he was named as Giovanni di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, a second cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent. With no sure portrait of Giovanni to compare, the name has been called uncertain, though Christie's sold the picture under it in 1982. He looks younger than the age at which Renaissance men usually married, and he may be cast as a youthful lover.

details.text: Look at the saint: an old man with a long grey beard and a halo, one hand raised, set against stamped and tooled gold. He may be the young man's name saint; Peter and John have both been suggested. Behind the youth there is no gold at all, only open blue air beyond a window.

In an earlier Botticelli portrait, now in the Uffizi and dating from the mid-1470s, the sitter shows us a medal of Cosimo de' Medici, and this panel may once have been built the same way. It has also been argued that the opening held not a medal but a mirror. If so, the woman meant to look at his portrait would have seen her own face in his hands, the idea behind the mirror-medals of the time, with a man's portrait on one side and polished metal on the other.

context.text: Baroque painting often makes a scene feel as though it is unfolding before us, through movement, dramatic lighting and forceful gesture. Rome was a major starting point, with Caravaggio and Annibale Carracci offering different models. Catholic commissions helped the style develop, but the term also encompasses secular painting and work made in Protestant countries.

Classicism draws on ideals of order, clarity and harmony associated with ancient Greece and Rome. A painter can work in this tradition without copying an ancient object or choosing a classical story. It is a recurring approach to art, while Neoclassicism names a more specific historical revival in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

Seventeenth-century Dutch painters made portraits, landscapes, still lifes and scenes of daily life into major fields of specialisation. Close attention to light and surfaces could make familiar surroundings newly absorbing. Yet these pictures also take part in debates about religion, wealth and domestic conduct: their apparent everydayness does not make them neutral records.

Painters in the fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century Low Countries used extraordinarily precise detail to make people, objects and sacred events feel present. Jan van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden helped establish an international market for this art. Religious narrative and observation worked together: convincing rooms, fabrics and landscapes could bring a devotional image closer to its viewer.

In fifteenth-century Florence, painters approached the representation of the visible world with new rigour. Masaccio's generation shared an interest in naturalism and in the culture of ancient Greece and Rome with sculptors and architects such as Donatello and Brunelleschi. The period's innovations developed within existing religious and civic traditions, rather than replacing them all at once.

Around 1500–1520, Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael developed ways of giving complex groups a powerful sense of unity. Order, balance and the dignity of the human figure became lasting ideals for later artists. Rome and Venice joined Florence as major centres of patronage, though their painters pursued those ideals in distinct ways.

The Hudson River School grew from a circle of American landscape painters influenced by Thomas Cole. Its artists combined close study of nature with ambitious, often idealised views. Their subjects extended well beyond the Hudson Valley: Church and Bierstadt helped make distant and spectacular scenery central to the movement's public appeal.

context.text: The Impressionists brought changing light and contemporary experience into the foreground of painting. Broken brushwork and bright colour could suggest a moment's appearance without describing every detail. They were a varied circle rather than a school with one programme; their eight independent exhibitions in Paris, from 1874 to 1886, offered an alternative to the official Salon.

Around 1400, painters and ideas moved between the courts of Europe, and a shared style grew out of the exchange. Elegant, courtly figures appear among delicately observed flowers and animals. The Wilton Diptych, painted for the English king Richard II, shows how mixed the style was. Nobody knows who painted it, and guesses at the artist's homeland range from England and France to Italy and Bohemia. Gentile da Fabriano, one of its finest painters, was working in Florence in the 1420s. In Barcelona, Bernat Martorell was still painting in the manner in the 1430s.

Neoclassical artists looked to ancient Greece and Rome for models of clarity, order and seriousness. Archaeological discoveries and illustrated publications helped renew that interest in the later eighteenth century. Ancient subjects could also speak to contemporary politics, as in David's painting, although the movement ranged from his severity to much gentler forms of classicism.

North of the Alps, Renaissance art developed through exchanges among local traditions and new ideas from Italy. Artists such as Dürer studied perspective, anatomy and classical forms, then adapted them to their own purposes. Humanist scholarship and, in the sixteenth century, the Reformation also changed the settings in which images were made and understood.

Post-Impressionism groups together several different responses to Impressionism. Cézanne explored pictorial structure, Gauguin the suggestive power of colour and line, van Gogh emotional expression, and Seurat a systematic approach to colour. These artists did not share a single style or programme; the name was coined later, for Roger Fry's London exhibition of 1910.

In nineteenth-century France, Realism challenged the prestige of idealised historical and mythological subjects by taking contemporary life seriously. Courbet was central to that challenge. Ordinary people and their work could become substantial subjects for painting. The movement's name is more specific than the everyday use of realism to mean a convincing likeness.

Renaissance means rebirth: the term recalls a renewed interest in ancient Greek and Roman culture. In painting, that interest accompanied new approaches to naturalism and the organisation of pictorial space. Its development was gradual and uneven, and religious art remained central. The label covers several centuries and many regional traditions, rather than one uniform style.

Rococo developed in early eighteenth-century France, bringing lightness and intimacy to painting and decoration. Curving forms, delicate colour and playful or amorous subjects are often associated with it. Watteau, Boucher and Fragonard each gave those possibilities a different character; the label need not imply that every picture is carefree.

Romanticism gave particular weight to imagination and individual experience. It could find its subjects in extraordinary events, distant times or the encounter with nature. Its artists differed widely in technique and outlook; even the familiar opposition to Neoclassicism is incomplete, since both could pursue ideals of grandeur and heroic feeling.

Colour, light and atmosphere became central concerns of Venetian Renaissance painting. Giovanni Bellini and the generations that followed him developed ways of making forms belong to a shared glow, as well as defining them by outlines. Venice's prosperity and its links through trade made it an important setting for this art, with a character distinct from Florence and Rome.

Pointillism describes paint applied in small, separate touches, especially in the work of Seurat and his followers. It is a method of handling paint. Divisionism refers more specifically to the separation of colours and the theory behind it; the two terms overlap but are not interchangeable.

cross.name: Cross
cross.text: The cross connects Christian images to Christ's Crucifixion. Different forms can also help identify saints: the diagonal cross is associated with Andrew, and the T-shaped cross with Antony the Great. In images of the infant Christ, a cross can anticipate the Passion still to come.
